The Robotics Fieldbook · Home survey edition

Build a robot.
Give it a sense
of place.

Design the parts. Make the wheels turn. Train a model. Build a measured map of one real room—and a path toward a robot that understands your home.

You already know how to build software. This book starts where the physical world makes that experience interesting: a printed hole that grips too tightly, a wheel that turns without travelling as far as expected, and a model that recognizes the carpet instead of the toy. We will make those effects observable, then change one thing and check what happened.

Our working vision is a home robot with spatial memory. It measures its surroundings, moves to selected places, and connects observations with context. Eventually you might ask it about a room or give it a useful task. The first finish line is smaller and concrete: a custom rover surveys one room, produces a checked metric map, completes a short waypoint trip, and records predictions from a model you trained.

Start at your workbench. It keeps your current session, the evidence you saved, and your exact next action together. Your first session chooses a test room and target toy; photographs and a measured print follow. Open your workbench →

This page holds the larger vision. For an ordinary work session, use your workbench: open the current task, check what you need, and work toward its small finish condition. Each session explains which robot capability it supports. The full chapters, roadmap and resource library remain nearby when you need context.

The course is built around your actual starting point

You have fifteen-plus years of programming experience and use coding agents. You have designed single parts in Fusion, printed your own and downloaded designs, and wired Arduino LEDs. Assemblies, powered motion, SLAM, and training models are new. We explain those foundations directly and use your software skills to inspect the evidence.

Your bench has an X1 Carbon and normal measuring, soldering, and hand tools. Your Windows 11 machine has an RTX 4090; the GB10 Spark is on your LAN. We begin the learning code on CPU so you can verify it immediately, then enable acceleration deliberately. A modest native Ubuntu computer on the eventual rover handles sensor connections and local control. The desktop machines can process recorded data.

Most sessions target 45–60 minutes of active work. Prints, downloads, and hardware integration may take longer. Session estimates are planning aids, not deadlines. Optional evenings are available for curiosity; the core route fits into ordinary workday sessions.

One route, two tracks

The workbench follows the route below a session at a time. There is one deliberate early handoff: make the Chapter 02 fit coupon, train the Chapter 03 models while parts arrive, then finish the Chapter 02 assembly before Chapter 04. The diagram shows why the work belongs together. You start collecting training data before the drivetrain arrives, and train the first model before building the full mapping stack.

Keep the larger ideas visible

Gaussian splats, voxel geometry, richer segmentation, conversational tasks, basket transport, and exercise games belong beyond the core milestones. Save a new idea from your workbench with the session that inspired it, then return to the action you had open. When a capability is ready, those ideas become candidates for the next experiment. The earlier joint, snake, and simulated locomotion material is preserved in the previous-edition workshop.

The finish line has evidence

CapabilityWhat you show
Make and assembleA repeatable fit log, editable Fusion assembly, accessible fasteners, and a mechanically secure rover.
Move dependablyDocumented wheel direction/counts, manually measured motion, and demonstrated stopping after stale commands and lost communication.
Measure a roomA replayable recording, a saved map, and several independent reference distances with their errors reported.
NavigateA supervised short waypoint run in the bounded test area, including a deliberately placed obstacle and a cancel/stop test.
Train and interpretA dataset manifest, baseline and neural artifacts, validation decisions, reserved-test results, and examples of failures.
Remember an observationA queryable record containing the source image, time, map revision, capture pose, and model version.

For measuring, our purpose is understanding layout. A horizontal lidar slice cannot capture ceiling height or every surface, and a map that looks tidy does not establish dimensional accuracy. We will measure errors before deciding what the result is useful for.

A vision you can explain at work

Hypothesis: a mobile observer could help people keep useful, current knowledge of their home. The first research question is whether it can produce trustworthy spatial observations. Later, we ask whether those observations answer a recurring question well enough that someone uses the system again. A plausible prototype and demonstrated customer value are separate forms of evidence.

The project does not have a fixed budget yet. Chapter 04 sets out a staged reference architecture and the checks required before each purchase. You can complete the first data and fit experiments with equipment already at hand.

Checkpoint: write the first finish line in your project notes and name the room and object you will use. The complete robot and its printed chassis have not been physically built or verified for this edition; the book distinguishes executable desktop exercises from hardware integration work.

Do this next: open your workbench →

01 · Give the robot a place and a question

A room to measure.
A toy to recognize.

We are building a rover that can survey a room and remember what it saw. Your first contribution is a small reference kit: a measured room sketch, labelled photographs, and a real part to test against a print.

Start the guided first session and record your result →

Picture the later result: you ask what the rover noticed near a marked place in the room, and it can show you an image, a capture time, and the position it was observing from. That starts with two things we can check ourselves: where the room's surfaces are, and whether one specific object is visible in a photograph. Today you make those reference observations before asking a robot or model to reproduce them.

There are three working sessions below. Do one at a time; together they may take more than an hour. Session 01A produces notes/room-reference.md. Session 01B produces twenty image files and notes/capture-A.md. Session 01C produces a measured row in notes/fit-log.csv. You do not need a built robot or new hardware purchases to start the room and image work.

The first model answers a question about the whole image: “Is this particular toy visible?” We will later connect that prediction to the rover's capture pose. A positive answer will not locate the toy within the image, prove the floor is safe to drive across, or establish that the toy is still there now.

Session 01A · Define the room your rover will learn

20–35 minutes of active work · Phone or camera, tape measure, paper and a text editor · Result: one room-reference note with three measured spans and a target-object rule

Your objective: make a reference that another person could use to identify your test area, repeat your three measurements, and label a photograph of your chosen toy.

Those measurements will later give us an independent way to check the robot's map.

  1. Choose the first test area and the object. Use one room, or a clearly bounded part of a room, with three accessible distances you can measure. A clear patch of hardwood is a useful starting place. Pick one distinctive, movable toy: for example, a particular brightly coloured block or small figure. Record: the room/boundary and “The first learned observation is whether [this specific object] is visibly present.” Keep this rule fixed through the first model comparison. An unclear or heavily hidden object is a reason to retake an image, not guess its label.
  2. Create the local place for this work. In File Explorer, create home-rover somewhere you can find again, then create notes, cad, data, and runs inside it. All paths in the course are relative to that folder. This is your robot project's working folder, separate from the textbook's GitHub repository. Create notes/room-reference.md in your text editor and copy the blank template below. In Windows Notepad, use Save as type → All files so the name does not become room-reference.md.txt. Record: your actual folder path and the two decisions from step 1. Keep household images and large recordings local by default; if you use Git, exclude those files rather than committing the entire working folder.
  3. Make the room recognizable on paper. Photograph the test area. Draw a top-down outline on paper or in a drawing tool; a rough sketch is enough. Mark fixed features such as wall faces, a door jamb, or a cabinet face. Mark the chosen test boundary if you are using only part of the room. Save a photograph or image of the sketch beside the room photograph in notes/. Record: both file paths. For eventual powered trials, the rover stays on this floor: stair access will be physically blocked and the test area will be clear of children and pets.
  4. Measure three spans you can repeat. Label them R1, R2, and R3 on your sketch. Choose one longer span and two shorter spans, with at least two directions represented. For each span, mark its start and end surfaces, hold the tape along a straight line, and read the distance. Keep the measuring height consistent for that span; do not silently swap a wall face for a protruding skirting board. Record the height or other detail another person would need to place the tape the same way. Record: the two endpoints, the measured length in metres, the tool, and the method or limitation for every span. Recheck any reading whose endpoint or tape alignment is uncertain.
  5. Check your reference against the room. Open the saved note and sketch, then point to the actual start and end of each span. Check that the object rule identifies one particular toy. Record: the date and any unresolved limitation, such as a cabinet preventing a wall-to-wall measurement. Keep the true boundary of what you measured: a distance across part of the room is not automatically the room's full width.

Save as notes/room-reference.md. Replace every bracket with your own decision, path, or observation. The blank lengths are places for your measurements.

# First room reference
Date: [date]
Project folder: [full local path to home-rover]
Room / test boundary: [where this first survey begins and ends]
Why this area: [one reason it is manageable]

Target object: [identify the particular toy]
Label rule: The first learned observation is whether [object] is visibly present.
Ambiguous image rule: Retake the image if a person cannot confidently apply the rule.

Room photograph: [relative path beneath notes/]
Labelled sketch: [relative path beneath notes/]
Tool: [tape measure or other actual tool]

| Span | Start surface | End surface | Measured length (m) | Height / alignment / method |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | [fill in] | [fill in] | [measure] | [fill in] |
| R2 | [fill in] | [fill in] | [measure] | [fill in] |
| R3 | [fill in] | [fill in] | [measure] | [fill in] |

Limitations or readings to recheck: [actual limitation, or none observed]
Future powered-test boundary: [how stair access and the test area will be controlled]

Check the result: your note identifies the test boundary and target rule, links the photo/sketch, and records three measured spans with endpoints, units, and method. Someone using it can point to the same endpoints in the room. Keep uncertain readings marked as uncertain.

You now have something the future map can be compared against. The next session reuses the same toy and label rule to begin your model's training data.

Session 01B · Collect the first twenty examples

25–40 minutes of active work · The chosen toy and an existing camera · Result: ten present images, ten absent images, and one capture note

Your objective: save ten photographs with the chosen toy visibly present, ten with it absent, and a note identifying the capture conditions.

The label should follow the toy's presence. If every present image has one background and every absent image has another, a model could learn the backgrounds and appear to recognize the toy. Varying the scene within both labels helps us test what it learns. This is the first part of the dataset your own model will learn from while you build the rover.

A capture session is a related collection taken under one set of conditions. Neighbouring video frames often carry almost the same information. Later, we will keep whole sessions together when splitting data so that we can test whether the model handles views it has not already encountered.

  1. Prepare the two labels. Open your room-reference note and keep the target rule beside you. Inside home-rover/data, create train/A/present and train/A/absent. These folders hold the photographs; the capture note belongs in notes/capture-A.md. Record: session A, the date, and the camera you are using. A phone is sufficient.
  2. Make one present/absent pair. Put the toy where a person can clearly recognize it and take a photo. Remove that toy entirely and take another photo. Save the first in present and the second in absent. Use unique names such as A_001.jpg and A_002.jpg. Check now: open both saved files and apply your written rule; this catches an export or folder mistake before you take eighteen more pictures.
  3. Build ten varied pairs. Alternate between present and absent until each folder contains ten distinct images. Across the pairs, change viewpoint, camera distance, the toy's position in the frame, and background arrangement. Move unrelated objects around in both classes. Keep the target recognizable in positive examples. Record: the kinds of variation you introduced and the lighting/background conditions. Twenty near-identical burst frames are not the intended result.
  4. Inspect the files you will actually train with. Export ordinary JPEG or PNG files. Remove location metadata if you intend to share them, and avoid including people, documents, or screens unnecessarily. Open all twenty files. Correct a wrong folder, and recapture an ambiguous or unreadable image instead of guessing its label. Record: the readable count in each folder and any correction you made.
  5. Save the capture conditions and the boundary of this result. Complete the note below. Keep all images beneath the same home-rover/data directory. Record: one condition not covered yet—for example, another lighting setup or a different background. If you only managed a simpler set today, describe that accurately; do not duplicate files to fill the count.

Save as notes/capture-A.md. This note preserves the conditions and counts; you do not need to create the training manifest yet.

# Capture session A
Date: [date]
Camera / image format: [actual camera and JPEG or PNG]
Target object and label rule: [copy from room-reference.md]
Lighting / background: [what was actually present]
Viewpoint, distance and placement changes: [what you varied]

Present folder: data/train/A/present/
Readable present files: [count]
Absent folder: data/train/A/absent/
Readable absent files: [count]
Corrections or recaptures: [what changed, or none needed]
Condition this session does not cover: [one concrete limitation]
Assigned split: training

Keep the folder names as shown. Chapter 03 will generate data/manifest.csv after the full collection exists. A manifest is a table that tells the training program where each image lives, which capture session it belongs to, and which label it has. The generated rows will resemble the following illustration; do not create this partial CSV now.

path,session,split,label
train/A/present/A_001.jpg,A,train,1
train/A/absent/A_002.jpg,A,train,0

The complete experiment will collect sessions A–H: A–D for training, E–F for validation while choosing the model, and G–H for the reserved final test. Every session contains both labels. Twenty images per session is an initial collection target, not a promise that 160 images will solve household recognition. Today you only need session A.

Check the result: ten distinct present files and ten distinct absent files open correctly, agree with your label rule, and are in the matching session folders. The capture note records their conditions and counts. Session A is useful saved data; the complete training program still needs the later validation and test sessions.

The model track now has its first real input. Next, we will give the mechanical track an equally concrete reference: the part a printed opening must fit.

Session 01C · Measure the part your first print must fit

15–20 minutes of active work · Calipers and a real M3 bolt or smooth pin · Result: one measured mating-part row in the fit log

Your objective: save repeatable measurements of a physical part you will keep beside the printer.

A label such as “M3” identifies a hardware family; it does not tell us which opening in your printed coupon will accept that particular bolt.

  1. Choose and label one part. Use an M3 bolt if you have one; it will test the clearance strip in Chapter 02. A smooth pin is also useful, provided you record what it is and choose a matching coupon later. Keep the part in a labelled bag or small container. Record: a specimen ID such as bolt-A, the feature to measure, and the nominal size only if it is known.
  2. Check the measuring tool. Clean the outside caliper jaws, close them gently, and check zero. Set millimetres. Measure across the bolt's thread crests or the smooth pin's outside diameter with light, consistent contact. Avoid measuring a bolt head when you intend to fit its threaded body. Record: the tool and zero-check result.
  3. Take three readings. Measure the diameter, release the jaws, rotate or reposition the part, and measure again. Repeat once more. Keep the jaws square to the feature. Record: all three readings in millimetres and where/direction they were taken; do not replace them with the nominal size. If the readings differ noticeably, recheck zero and contact before deciding that the part or printer is inaccurate.
  4. Save a row for the actual mating part. Download the fit-log template and save it as notes/fit-log.csv. Open it in a spreadsheet or text editor. Add a new row for your labelled part. Use specimen_id and feature to identify it; put the three readings in actual_1_mm, actual_2_mm, and actual_3_mm. Put tool, zero check, and contact directions in notes. The supplied pin-A and coupon rows are for later printed specimens; do not relabel them as a bolt you measured today. Leave print settings and printed-fit results blank until those checks happen.
  5. Name the next print. Open the X1 Carbon recipe session. With the M3 bolt, the next fit experiment uses the clearance strip; save its name in your fit-log notes and keep the same bolt for that test. If using a different pin, record the matching coupon choice and any geometry you still need to check. Record: the coupon decision and the saved fit-log path. You will choose and save the actual printer recipe in the next session, before printing.

Check the result: the saved log identifies the real part, contains three actual readings with units and method, and names the next small print. You can retrieve the same physical part. No printed clearance has been established yet.

You now have three small, useful artifacts: room measurements to check a map, photographs to teach a model, and a mating part to check a print. The next physical step is to save a repeatable X1 Carbon recipe and print the smallest uncertain fit. While that print runs, the image collection can grow in parallel.

Next: save the X1 Carbon recipe for your first fit test →

Chapter 02 · Hardware track

Design a chassis
that fits.

A pair of wheels needs to hold its alignment. A scanner needs a steady view. Your first assembly gives both a place to live.

We are building a small survey rover for a bounded patch of hardwood floor. Two powered wheels steer it by turning at different speeds; a third contact supports the body. The first chassis carries its own components. Laundry, thresholds, and climbing loads belong to later designs. We will learn more from a removable motor bracket and a measured mounting hole than from an elaborate shell that hides the wires.

You have designed individual parts in Fusion. The next skill is preserving relationships between parts: the wheels share an axle line, the deck clears their tyres, the support keeps the body level, and each component can be removed. We will start from real dimensions and print the smallest uncertain fit before printing an entire deck.

What is supplied: the small fit coupons and measurement sheets are downloadable below. The new survey chassis is a guided custom-design exercise; a finished, physically validated CAD assembly is not supplied. The old TT-motor deck belongs to the archived first rover and does not match this drivetrain.

Choose the reference drivetrain

The default uses two Pololu #4885 47:1 low-power 12 V encoder gearmotors, a pair of #2676 metal motor brackets, and #3690 80 mm wheels with their 4 mm D-shaft collets. The bracket and wheel interfaces are purchased; your deck, equipment trays, and sensor mounts are the design work. This keeps the first precision exercise focused on accessible printed features.

A RoboClaw controller, motor battery, and small onboard computer will need room too. We will specify their electrical interfaces in Chapter 04. For now, use the component build sheet to record actual dimensions, mass, connectors, and mounting patterns. It is a staged specification, not a promise that every currently sold variation fits together. Confirm the exact part revision before ordering the matching mount.

Session · Save an X1 Carbon baseline

15 minutes setup · Plain PLA and the installed build plate · Output: a repeatable print recipe

Use the PLA you already print successfully. Select the actual X1 Carbon nozzle and plate in Bambu Studio; the starting geometry assumes a 0.4 mm nozzle. Start from 0.20 mm Standard, three walls, four top and bottom layers, 20% infill, normal speed, and supports off for the flat coupons. Save a copy as X1C-survey-PLA-baseline and save the arranged print as a 3MF project.

Keep the matching filament preset and plate preparation guidance. Record the filament, nozzle, plate, process version, and material batch in your fit log. Follow the Studio guidance for chamber ventilation with PLA and your plate. Changing material, orientation, nozzle, or process later means checking important fits again.

For the first fit experiment, set manual X-Y hole and contour compensation to zero; leave automatic circle compensation off if your version offers it. Record the existing elephant-foot compensation. These controls address different geometry errors. Bambu's compensation reference is useful when diagnosing a repeatable error; it does not supply a universal tolerance for your printer.

Done: the saved project identifies the actual printer configuration and a single material. Automatic calibration and a neat-looking print are useful process signals; neither proves a mating part will fit.

Session · Print a small question

30 minutes active work plus printing · Calipers and an M3 screw · Output: a measured fit

Download the 40 × 20 × 4 mm clearance strip. Its open slots are nominally 2.8, 3.0, 3.2, and 3.4 mm, left to right with the openings facing away from you. Print it flat with the unchanged baseline. While it prints, return to the image collection in Chapter 03.

  1. After cooling, label the slots. Slide the threaded portion of an actual M3 screw into each slot with light finger pressure. Do not cut a thread by turning it. Record the smallest comfortable fit.
  2. Zero the calipers, then repeat measurements at the top and bottom of the strip. Look for a first-layer lip. Repeat each reading rather than treating the display resolution as measurement accuracy.
  3. Print the round-hole coupon and 6 mm test pin when a round fit matters. Hold the coupon's clipped corner at upper right: its nearby row is 3.0, 3.2, 3.4, 3.6, 3.8 mm, and the other row is 6.0, 6.2, 6.4, 6.6 mm, both left to right. Print the coupon flat and the pin standing on its broad base.
  4. Measure the pin at two heights and directions; inspect the seam separately. Try the holes without forcing. Keep the first passing pair and repeat it before transferring the fit to a larger mount.

A hole 6.25 mm across around a 6.05 mm shaft leaves 0.20 mm diametral clearance. If centred, that is 0.10 mm on each side. Those numbers are an example, not measurements of the supplied STL. A supported sideways hole can behave differently from this vertical hole, so test the orientation you intend to use.

Done: you can show a fitting pair and its measured dimensions, material, and orientation. Keep that pair beside the printer. It is your evidence for this local design choice.

Default route: after the fit coupon, go to Chapter 03 and train your first models. The remaining layout, Fusion mount and assembly sessions below are your return point once component drawings and parts are available. Complete them before Chapter 04.

Session · Make the robot fit on paper

45–60 minutes active work · Fusion, ruler, component drawings · Output: an assembly layout

Start a Fusion design in millimetres. Create separate components named deck, left_drive, right_drive, support, and electronics. A component represents a replaceable thing; it is more useful here than one body containing every shape. Put the origin halfway between the wheel contact centres on the nominal floor plane. We will later use x forward, y left, and z up in the robot software. In this coordinate system the floor is z = 0; the deck needs a positive height above it.

Place the first part in three dimensions

A top view can hide a deck that passes through the floor. Establish the side view before adding detail. In Modify → Change Parameters, add the following named lengths in millimetres. The 40 mm radius below is an illustration from an unloaded 80 mm wheel; use your measured component geometry for the design.

ParameterMeaning and source
wheel_radiusAxle height above the nominal floor. Start with the wheel drawing and check the loaded assembly later.
axle_to_deck_bottomSigned vertical distance from motor-shaft centre to the deck's underside, determined by the chosen bracket orientation and drawing.
deck_bottom_zwheel_radius + axle_to_deck_bottom. This is the offset of the deck sketch plane above the floor.
deck_thickness4 mm as an initial prototype thickness; it does not establish a rated load.

For example, a hypothetical bracket placing the deck underside 15 mm above an axle at 40 mm produces deck_bottom_z = 55 mm. Those are teaching values, not dimensions of the selected Pololu bracket. Verify the real distance and sign from its drawing and delivered part.

  1. Activate the deck component. Choose Construct → Offset Plane, select the XY origin plane, and enter deck_bottom_z. Sketch a provisional 220 × 180 mm deck rectangle on that plane, then extrude upward by deck_thickness. Inspect a side view: the wheels reach the floor and the deck clears it.

After the next mounting-coupon session creates the actual attachment geometry, use the rigid-joint exercise below to preserve the bracket’s relationship to the deck.

The distinction between a sketch constraint and an assembly joint matters here: the constraint controls geometry inside a component; the joint controls the relationship between components. Use Autodesk's offset-plane instructions, joint instructions, and grounding reference only as each operation becomes relevant. The wheel can remain a static envelope during this packaging exercise.

  1. Treat the initial deck size as a packaging trial that fits within the X1C's build area, not a required final size or a rated structural design. Use simple boxes and cylinders for the purchased components; include plug and cable-bend space.
  2. Place the motor axes on the same transverse line, with wheels outside the deck. Keep the motor bodies accessible from below and leave room to remove the wheel. Measure the wheel-centre separation; name it track_width. It is not the deck width.
  3. Place the third contact ahead of the axle line and put heavy components low, between the support contacts. Viewed from above, the projected centre of mass should remain inside their support triangle. Leave a clear route to the power disconnect.
  4. Reserve a stable upper location for the lidar with an unobstructed horizontal scan. Reserve a forward camera mount and cable route. A tall, flexible mast makes every bump look like sensor motion, so begin short and stiff.
  5. Draw the actual fastener heads, washers, nuts, and tool access as clearance envelopes. Choose two bracket mounting points separated as widely as the bracket permits. Use its current drawing and your measurement; this bracket family has had different hole spacing across revisions.

Done: the layout has a shared axle line, room for cables, three support contacts, and a reachable fastener for every replaceable component. Save a screenshot with the front direction marked. If two parts collide, move their simple envelopes now.

Session · Turn the successful fit into a mount

45–60 minutes active work · Fusion and one delivered bracket · Output: a mounting coupon

Reuse deck_thickness and add named parameters for screw_clearance, pocket_clearance_per_side, and the measured bracket-hole spacing. The 4 mm deck remains a starting prototype thickness. Choose the clearance from your coupon instead of copying a number from another printer. Keep overall dimensions separate from mating clearances so a tight pocket does not tempt you to scale the whole assembly.

  1. Model only the deck region under one motor bracket: a small plate with its two selected mounting holes and enough surrounding material for washers. Position the holes from the bracket drawing, then verify against the delivered part.
  2. Constrain the sketch and use dimensions rather than dragging geometry into place. Extrude the plate; cut the holes; add a small lead-in where it helps insertion. Keep the bracket as a separate component.
  3. Export a mesh in millimetres with enough refinement that holes are visibly round in the slicer. Inspect the imported dimensions. Print the coupon in the same orientation intended for the deck.
  4. Assemble with through-bolts, washers, and nuts. The screw passes through the plastic; the nut supplies the thread. Tighten only enough to hold the bracket without crushing the plastic. Confirm that a driver can reach both screws and the bracket can be removed.
  5. Transfer the passing hole pattern into the complete deck. Add local ribs or wider mounting pads where loads enter. Inspect the layer preview around those regions; extra infill elsewhere will not repair a narrow, weak mounting tab.

Keep the fitted bracket attached in CAD

  1. Fix the deck component to the design using Pin (called Ground in older interfaces). Keep the bracket component free to move; remove an automatic Ground To Parent relationship from that component if necessary. Ground To Parent fixes a child relative to its parent, while Pin fixes its position in the design.
  2. With the deck and bracket represented by separate components, choose Assemble → Joint and Rigid. Select matching attachment locations on the bracket and deck—such as the centres of mating screw holes—and check the preview's face orientation and offset before accepting. A rigid joint removes relative motion between these bolted parts.
  3. Try dragging the bracket and inspect the side view again. It should stay attached to the pinned deck without an unexplained gap. If the bracket is already correctly positioned, an As-Built Joint → Rigid can preserve that position; it does not correct a misplaced part.

Read the orientation and assembly sections of Prusa's design guide with one question: which surface needs an accurate fit, and which direction loads it? Its geometric advice is useful across printers; machine-specific performance claims do not establish your X1C result.

Done: the bracket fits without forcing, stays located under a gentle hand load, and can be removed. Save the native Fusion design and the slicer project together.

Choose the third contact from the geometry: use a small purchased swivel caster with a bolted plate and a documented load rating above the load it will support. Measure the floor-to-mount-plane distance with the drive wheels fitted. Subtract the caster’s installed height to obtain the required spacer thickness; a negative result means that caster is too tall for this layout. Check the full swivel envelope in Fusion and test rolling resistance on hardwood. Record its exact part number and mounting drawing before printing the deck. The old rover’s caster spacers are not automatically correct for this new assembly.

Session · Assemble the rolling structure

45–60 minutes active work plus printing · Unpowered components · Output: a chassis that rolls without rubbing

Print the full deck after the local fit passes. Mount the motors using the supplied bracket-to-motor screws; excessive engagement can reach the gears. Fit the wheel's correct 4 mm D-shaft collet using the wheel maker's assembly instructions, supporting the mechanism rather than hammering the shaft. Keep wheels close enough to their supports to avoid needless overhang, with clearance for the tyre and hub to rotate.

Install the third contact using measured spacers so the deck sits level. Roll the unpowered assembly by hand over clean hardwood. Mark one point on each wheel and watch for wobble or a tyre rubbing the deck. Move the caster through its full swivel arc and check wires cannot enter a wheel. Temporarily secure representative component masses where they will actually sit, then repeat the roll check. This is a prototype inspection, not a payload rating.

Trace the load from floor to tyre, shaft, motor bracket, deck, and payload. A sensor tray that moves relative to the chassis changes the sensor's assumed position. Add bracing at the moving joint, reduce its height, or widen its support before increasing print infill. Keep ventilation openings and the physical disconnect accessible.

Done: the unpowered loaded layout sits on three contacts, rolls without visible binding, retains its parts, and has accessible fasteners. Record the overall footprint, loaded wheel radius estimate, and wheel-centre separation. We will calibrate rolling measurements after powered movement works.

If a part does not fit, take the small loop

ObservationNext action
Only the bottom edge catchesCompare top and bottom dimensions; inspect elephant foot and first-layer conditions. Change one relevant setting in a copy and reprint the coupon.
A slot or pocket is tight through its full depthIncrease that feature's CAD clearance. An open slot is not an enclosed hole, so hole compensation is the wrong control.
Several vertical holes are consistently undersizedConfirm the measurement and print quality, then compare a small manual hole-compensation trial. A boundary offset changes the diameter on both sides.
A sideways hole sags or the deck liftsChange orientation, support, or bed adhesion before applying dimensional compensation.
The deck flexes near a fastenerInspect the load path, washer support, and local rib geometry. A larger global scale changes every useful dimension.

Keep the evidence

Save the measured fit, one assembly photo, your Fusion revision, and the build sheet. Your next physical task is one powered wheel. If you have not completed the parallel learning experiment yet, return to train a model from your first labelled images.

03 · A real training experiment

Teach it one visual distinction.

Your rover is still taking shape. Meanwhile, you can collect examples, fit a model, and find out what it actually learned.

Choose one distinctive toy already in your home. Our first question is deliberately concrete: “Is this particular toy visible in this image?” You will train a simple classifier, then a small neural network, and compare their mistakes. Later, the rover can attach these predictions to camera observations on its map.

This is supervised learning: you supply images and correct labels, and an algorithm adjusts model parameters to reduce prediction error. A trained classifier returns one label for the entire image. It does not yet locate the toy, identify every kind of toy, decide whether tidying is needed, or establish a clear driving route. Those are additional tasks with different evidence requirements.

Our finish line

You have a frozen dataset, a baseline, a neural-network checkpoint that reloads correctly, and an evaluation you can explain. A weak model still gives us a completed experiment when we can identify its limitations. Household recognition performance has not been established for this starter.

Download the complete model-training starter ↓

The ZIP contains learn.py, a manifest generator, pinned supporting dependencies, a dataset-schema example, a README, and executable synthetic checks. Extract those files directly into the home-rover project directory you created in Chapter 01, beside its existing data/ directory. Reuse your session A images; keep one project and dataset tree. You can begin with a phone; preserve which camera captured each session so we can later measure the change to the rover camera.

Complete this first runnable training experiment while the hardware build is still underway. An assembled rover is not a prerequisite. After the model comparison, the default route returns to the chassis layout and assembly in Chapter 02.

Session 03A · Give the experiment a fair question

45–60 minutes per visit · Continue the collection begun in Chapter 01 · Artifact: a versioned image dataset

Put the same toy on the floor, photograph it, remove it, and photograph the scene again. Repeat from different positions. If every positive picture includes your hand and every negative picture does not, the easiest useful pattern may be your hand. The computer follows the evidence we give it.

  1. Write a one-sentence label rule: 1 = the chosen toy is visibly identifiable; 0 = it is absent. Set aside ambiguous or heavily obscured cases for a later experiment. Keep the target identity fixed.
  2. Continue from the session A images captured in Chapter 01. Complete eight independently varied capture sessions, A–H, with an initial target of ten present and ten absent images in each. Change viewpoint, placement, and scene arrangement within each session; vary conditions between sessions. This gives 160 starter examples, not a claim of sufficient data.
  3. Assign A–D to training, E–F to validation, and G–H to final testing before fitting anything. A session is a real capture occasion and setup. Splitting one video into differently named clips does not make its neighboring frames independent.
  4. Use data/train/A/absent/ and data/train/A/present/, then the corresponding directories for the remaining sessions. Validation and test use their own top-level directories. Export phone images as JPEG, PNG, or WebP. Keep the original captures separately.
  5. Our model receives 64 × 64 pixels. In Session 03B, the supplied inspection command will show training images at that exact resolution. If the toy disappears at that scale, capture a closer view for this first experiment. Preserve the same resizing rule during training and inference.

The training set adjusts model parameters. Validation helps us choose an approach and checkpoint. The reserved test set estimates performance after those decisions are frozen. The reason for grouping by session is practical: two adjacent camera frames can look almost identical, so random image splitting can reward remembering a scene.

Read the grouped-data section of scikit-learn’s evaluation guide. Return when you can explain why a frame from session A should not quietly appear in both training and testing.

Done: each session contains both labels, its split is declared, and you can show varied positive and negative examples. If collection needs another visit, record the next missing session and return to your mechanical task.

Session 03B · Run the pipeline on your Windows workstation

45–60 minutes · Python 3.12 and the extracted starter · Artifact: a checked environment and manifest

Start on CPU so that your first result depends on a small software stack. The Windows 11 workstation is the default host for this lesson. Python 3.12 must already be installed; open PowerShell in home-rover, where learn.py and data/ now sit beside each other, and run:

py -3.12 -m venv .venv
$LearnerPython = ".\.venv\Scripts\python.exe"
& $LearnerPython -m pip install -r requirements.txt
& $LearnerPython -m pip install torch==2.7.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
& $LearnerPython smoke_test.py
& $LearnerPython make_manifest.py data
& $LearnerPython learn.py check data/manifest.csv
& $LearnerPython learn.py inspect data/manifest.csv --out reports/train-inputs.png

The explicit Python path avoids needing an activation script. Set $LearnerPython again in each new terminal. Generate data/manifest.csv once after completing the collection. It uses path,session,split,label; image paths are relative to the CSV’s directory. Inspect the generated records against your folders. The generator refuses to overwrite an existing manifest so that changing the dataset is a deliberate revision. The supplied template is a schema reference, not a second manifest to maintain.

The checker rejects missing labels, sessions crossing splits, duplicate file paths, identical file bytes, and unreadable images. Malformed records name the CSV row or image to repair. It cannot detect every near-duplicate or an incorrect human label. The synthetic smoke check creates disposable colored patterns; passing it establishes code-path behavior, not recognition of your home.

Open reports/train-inputs.png. It shows the actual 64 × 64 inputs, enlarged twofold without smoothing, with your labels. Identify the toy in several positive examples; check whether absent examples accidentally share a different background. The default preview uses training images only. Its numbered JSON sidecar preserves full paths, and --limit 24 shows more examples. This is a view of the input, not a visualization of what the network attends to.

This recipe was exercised on Linux x86-64 with Python 3.12.14 and PyTorch 2.7.1+cpu. Windows and your hardware remain execution checks for your first session. The official previous-version instructions support reproducing the chosen release. After the CPU path works, use the official installation selector for a separate CUDA environment suitable for your RTX 4090 and driver, then verify torch.cuda.is_available(). The GB10 needs its own compatible environment; an x86-64 environment is not portable to it.

If the check stops: fix the first named file or session. Preserve the declared capture groups; changing a session ID merely to silence a leakage warning damages the experiment. If installation stalls, continue photographing or printing and leave the exact error in your restart note.

Session 03C · Train the simplest useful comparison

45–60 minutes · Checked dataset · Artifact: a saved baseline and validation report

& $LearnerPython learn.py train data/manifest.csv --kind baseline --out runs/baseline

The baseline compresses each image to a 16 × 16 RGB grid, standardizes those features using training data only, and fits logistic regression. Despite its name, logistic regression is a classifier here. It learns weights that combine the pixel features into a score for “present.” This already counts as training your own model.

Open runs/baseline/validation.json. Its confusion matrix has actual labels as rows and predicted labels as columns, ordered absent then present. A false positive is an absent image predicted present; a false negative is a present image predicted absent.

Generate the per-image validation report so you can inspect which pictures produced those errors:

& $LearnerPython learn.py evaluate data/manifest.csv runs/baseline --split validation --out runs/baseline/validation-details.json
& $LearnerPython learn.py inspect data/manifest.csv --split validation --report runs/baseline/validation-details.json --out reports/baseline-validation.png

Open the PNG to see mistakes first, followed by examples near the decision threshold. Each card shows the human label, prediction, and uncalibrated score for present. Open validation-details.json for all per-image predictions and per-session results. Paths are relative to data/. Compare a failed image with a correctly classified one; a visible difference gives you a hypothesis to test, rather than proof of what the model learned.

Balanced accuracy averages the two class recalls. If a model recognizes 9 of 10 absent images and 3 of 5 present images, its balanced accuracy is (0.9 + 0.6) / 2 = 0.75. This illustrative example makes the missed toys visible even when absent images dominate. An always-absent classifier scores 0.5 on this measure when both classes occur.

The saved scaler must also process later images: fitting a new scaler during evaluation changes the representation. Read scikit-learn’s preprocessing and leakage guidance, then locate the training-only StandardScaler.fit in learn.py.

Done: you can explain one error or inspect a boundary example when this validation set has no errors, and identify which data fitted the scaler. Keep the baseline even if the neural network later wins.

Session 03D · Train filters instead of specifying them

45–60 minutes · The same frozen dataset · Artifact: a neural checkpoint and learning history

& $LearnerPython learn.py train data/manifest.csv --kind cnn --out runs/cnn-7 --seed 7 --epochs 30

A convolutional neural network learns small filters that are applied across an image. Our starter has three convolution layers with ReLU nonlinearities, spatial averaging, and two output scores. Its weights start from random initialization; no pretrained model is downloaded. Inspect make_cnn() to connect that description to the actual layers.

Training measures prediction error with cross-entropy. For one positive example, assigning the correct class probability-like score 0.8 gives a loss of approximately −ln(0.8) = 0.223; assigning 0.2 gives about 1.609. These illustrative values explain why confidently wrong predictions receive a larger penalty. The gradient describes how the loss changes with each parameter, and the optimizer uses it to adjust the weights.

Open the training loop and find zero_grad(), loss.backward(), and optimizer.step(). Follow those three operations in the PyTorch optimization lesson. The goal is to explain the update, not memorize every derivative before proceeding.

The default uses Adam at learning rate 0.001, batches of 16 images, and at most 30 epochs. One epoch visits the training set once. Validation loss selects the saved checkpoint; five epochs without improvement stop the run early. Training class counts determine the training class weights. Test results do not choose the checkpoint.

Inspect history.csv, validation.json, and run.json. The run record preserves versions, seed, preprocessing, session assignment, and hashes of the dataset and script. Saved weights are reloaded and their predictions compared before training reports success. See PyTorch’s saving and loading lesson for the distinction between architecture and fitted parameters.

Create the same detailed validation view for the neural model:

& $LearnerPython learn.py evaluate data/manifest.csv runs/cnn-7 --split validation --out runs/cnn-7/validation-details.json
& $LearnerPython learn.py inspect data/manifest.csv --split validation --report runs/cnn-7/validation-details.json --out reports/cnn-validation.png

Compare the neural model’s input cards with the baseline’s on the same validation images; the JSON indexes preserve full paths when the two sheets sort differently. Both detailed reports include per-session metrics. Preserve them beside the aggregate reports; an existing output filename is intentionally not overwritten.

If the CNN loses: inspect its errors beside the baseline’s. Check object visibility after resizing, accidental background cues, and inconsistent labels. More layers are not the first repair for missing visual evidence. If training improves while validation worsens, the saved earlier checkpoint may be the useful result.

Done: compare both validation reports and explain one training-loop update. For a later stability check, predeclare seeds 7, 19, and 43 and report all three outcomes; do not keep rerolling until one looks good.

Session 03E · Find out what survived a new capture

45–60 minutes · Frozen comparison · Artifact: an honest model report

Write down the models and preprocessing you will compare, with the supplied threshold of 0.5, before opening final test reports. Then evaluate both fixed runs:

& $LearnerPython learn.py evaluate data/manifest.csv runs/baseline --out runs/baseline/test.json
& $LearnerPython learn.py evaluate data/manifest.csv runs/cnn-7 --out runs/cnn-7/test.json

Read per-session results as well as the pooled score. Inspect the individual wrong predictions. Keep the comparison even when the simpler model wins. A score from two small test sessions is limited evidence; it does not establish performance throughout your house.

Now that the fixed test evaluation exists, you can make its error sheet:

& $LearnerPython learn.py inspect data/manifest.csv --split test --report runs/cnn-7/test.json --out reports/cnn-test.png

Test and stress previews require a matching saved evaluation report; default input previews contain training images only. Each evaluation also records the evaluator’s code and package versions and hashes of the model configuration and weights. Inspect any same_script_as_training: false result before calling it the same frozen experiment: changed inspection prose and changed preprocessing have different consequences.

Once test errors influence a redesign, those sessions have become development data. Reserve fresh captures for the next final evaluation. The code prevents report overwrites and detects a changed dataset, but good experimental boundaries still depend on your decisions.

Finally, call learn.py predict runs/cnn-7 IMAGE_PATH with an actual image path. The result contains an uncalibrated score and a label. Later, collect new rover-camera sessions as a separate stress set and use the README’s --split stress workflow. Keep those results separate from the original test. A camera or lighting change is something we measure, not something a neural network automatically handles.

Let an agent help without losing the lesson

Ask: “Trace one image from this CSV through preprocessing, training, checkpoint selection, and inference. Show which information each step may use. Then find one way this evaluation could mislead me.” You own the labels, inspect the errors, and explain the conclusion. The agent can audit code and make a contact sheet.

Chapter complete: you have both fitted models, a reload check, frozen evaluation reports, and three sentences describing the best-supported result, an observed failure or untested condition, and the next useful data collection. The starter has been exercised with synthetic data; your household experiment supplies the real evidence.

Next: return to Chapter 02 and lay out your chassis →
If you already completed the layout, continue at mechanical assembly. Once that assembly passes its checks, proceed to Chapter 04 motor control.

Chapter 04 · Hardware track

Make motion
dependable.

Your first useful control system turns a small command into measured wheel movement—and stops when the command disappears.

The unpowered chassis tells us the parts fit. This chapter adds energy and feedback. We will bring up one wheel with your Windows computer, verify its encoder, repeat for the second wheel, and establish a bounded manual drive interface. Mapping comes after that interface can explain what the wheels actually did.

An encoder reports rotation; it cannot prove the tyre travelled the same distance along the floor. A velocity controller corrects wheel-speed error; it cannot notice a stair. Keeping those boundaries clear makes faults easier to locate. When the robot bends away from a straight line, we can ask separately whether its commands, wheel speeds, or traction differed.

Build status: the component interfaces below are supported by manufacturer documentation. This combined rover has not been assembled or physically tested for the book. The manufacturer software supplies the first-wheel bring-up. A ROS integration candidate and acceptance contract are supplied for the next stage; a validated, complete survey-rover driver/configuration is not bundled.

The reference electronics

Part or interfaceDefault and reason
Two drive motorsPololu #4885 LP 12 V encoder motors from Chapter 02. The nominal encoder specification is approximately 2,249 quadrature counts per output revolution; verify the controller's actual counting convention.
Local motor controlBasicmicro RoboClaw 2x7A, IMC404. It combines two motor channels, encoder inputs, local velocity feedback, and USB communication. Its current capability exceeds these motors' requirements; motor protection still needs configuration.
Motor powerA commercially assembled eight-cell NiMH pack, nominal 9.6 V, with a matched charger and documented current/connector rating. Verify its charged voltage is no more than 12 V before connecting this motor pair. Lower-than-nominal motor voltage reduces available performance; measure it on the real rover.
Power pathA fuse near battery positive, a reachable DC-rated positive-line disconnect, and properly terminated wiring. A 3 A fuse is a starting wiring-protection candidate only when the pack, connectors, switch, and wire are all rated appropriately; finalize its type and trip behaviour against the actual parts.
Robot computerA modest x86 mini-PC running native Ubuntu 24.04, with USB ports for controller and sensors. Verify Linux, USB, cooling, and supply compatibility before purchase. Use its manufacturer's supported power arrangement; the RoboClaw's 5 V, 800 mA output is not a PC supply.
Bench computer and connectionYour Windows 11 computer runs Motion Studio for initial setup. Use the manufacturer's USB isolation guidance, especially when motor and computer power have separate ground paths.

Keep motor power and computer power as two explicitly documented systems. A USB connector does not make their positive rails interchangeable. The build sheet records the voltage range, startup demand, connector polarity, and source for every item. Buy the drivetrain first; confirm the computer and sensor power arrangements before adding their weight to the deck.

Three electrical ideas for this build: voltage is the electrical supply condition across a component; current is the flow it draws under the present load. A motor usually draws more current as resisting torque increases. A stall is a powered motor whose shaft cannot turn, a condition that can heat it rapidly. For example, a 12 V supply capable of 7 A does not force 7 A through a motor; the motor and load determine the draw, and faults can demand more than small wiring or motors can tolerate. This is why we check both voltage and current limits before applying power.

Session · Draw the power path before wiring it

45–60 minutes · Battery disconnected · Output: a labelled wiring diagram and checked harness

Draw battery positive → fuse → disconnect → controller positive. Draw battery negative directly to controller negative. Then draw the motor outputs and the separate encoder supply. Use the controller's operational requirements to check the actual board revision, ratings, and disconnect arrangement. Remove positive power for a controlled shutdown; breaking only battery negative while USB is attached can create an unintended return path.

  1. With the pack unplugged, assemble the fuse holder, switch, and keyed connector. Use terminals suited to the actual screw terminals and conductor sizes; keep loose strands and unsupported splices away from the board. Secure the harness so pulling a cable does not pull its electrical contact.
  2. Use continuity mode only on the unpowered harness. Confirm each intended path and check that positive and negative are not shorted. A brief charging indication across controller capacitors is different from a persistent harness short; isolate the harness if the reading is unclear.
  3. Put the meter into DC voltage mode, with its leads in the voltage/common sockets. Measure the disconnected pack's polarity and voltage. A negative reading with the red probe on the intended positive contact means the connector or probe assignment needs correction. Do not place a current-mode meter across a battery.
  4. Record the pack's measured charged voltage and manufacturer discharge limits. Set controller voltage limits from that pack's documentation; use custom settings for the selected NiMH pack rather than an unrelated lithium-cell preset.
  5. Keep the wheels clear of the table on a stable stand. Leave both motor outputs disconnected for the first controller connection.

A regenerative controller can return energy from a slowing motor to its supply. A generic wall adapter may not absorb it. The chosen pack and controller limits must accommodate this behaviour; using a bench supply requires the manufacturer's documented clamp arrangement. This is why substituting a convenient adapter is a design change, even when its voltage label looks right.

Done: you can trace both supply conductors, identify the fuse and disconnect, and show the measured polarity before any motor turns.

Session · Connect one motor and read its encoder

45–60 minutes · Windows 11 and Motion Studio · Output: a verified direction and count

Disconnect power before wiring. For the specified Pololu motor, red and black are the motor pair. Green is encoder ground, blue is encoder supply, and yellow/white are channels A/B. Confirm those assignments against the exact motor page; colours from another motor are not an electrical standard. Supply this encoder from the controller's documented 5 V and ground pins, not the motor output.

Left motor connectionController destination
Red / black motor wiresM1A / M1B; adjust direction only with power removed or through documented configuration.
Green / blue encoder wiresEncoder ground / 5 V.
Yellow / white encoder signalsChannel 1 encoder A / B, using the board's labelled pinout.

The right motor will use M2A/M2B and encoder channel 2. Treat both motors as separate systems until each passes. Loose breadboard contacts are unsuitable for the motor-power path. Keep the encoder leads secured away from moving wheels and avoid routing a long loose bundle alongside the motor wiring.

  1. Install Motion Studio from the manufacturer downloads page. Power the controller from its main supply before connecting USB, then confirm its reported model, firmware, and voltage. Save those versions.
  2. Keep the output command at zero and turn the wheel slowly by hand. Observe whether the encoder changes. Mark the tyre and measure one output revolution; expect approximately 2,249 counts for the stated quadrature convention. Gear backlash and stopping exactly on the mark limit this hand check.
  3. Enable only channel 1 for a brief low-duty command with the wheel suspended. Observe direction and count sign. Define positive as the wheel motion that would drive the chassis forward. Verify the other direction, then command zero.
  4. If positive motion produces negative counts, correct the documented encoder direction setting before enabling velocity feedback. A feedback loop with the wrong sign can increase its command while trying to fix the apparent error.
  5. Power down, wire the second motor, and repeat. Label the cable groups LEFT and RIGHT and record the final motor/encoder direction configuration.

Use the manufacturer's quick-start guide to locate the controls on your installed version. USB supplies communication here; it is not the controller's main power source.

Done: each positive command and count agrees with your forward convention, turning one wheel changes only its corresponding encoder, and zero halts each wheel. Fill in the drive check log.

Session · Command a speed, then compare it with the measurement

One or more 45–60 minute sessions · Wheels supported first · Output: a low-speed response plot

The controller's PID loop adjusts motor output to reduce the difference between requested and measured encoder speed. Its parameters describe this motor, supply, and load. Follow Velocity Settings and the current tuning procedure for your revision. Automatic tuning can cause substantial motion; keep wheels supported, secure the chassis, and verify current and travel assumptions before invoking it.

The motor's extrapolated stall current at 12 V is 0.9 A. That is not a continuous operating target. Pololu's general continuous-current guidance is 25% of stall current or less, which is 0.225 A for this example. Begin with brief, unloaded low-output checks and a conservative current limit appropriate to the motor. Verify the controller can enforce and report the chosen limit; do not assume a high-current controller's sensing resolves small currents accurately enough without checking. If continuous loaded operation demands more current, reduce drag or payload and revisit the motor selection.

Plot the requested speed alongside measured speed during a small step and a return to zero. Start with a target corresponding to approximately 0.05 m/s at the floor, then inspect overshoot, settling, and current. Using an illustrative 80 mm rolling diameter, one revolution covers about 0.251 m; 0.05 m/s corresponds to roughly 447 encoder counts per second. The real rolling diameter and counted edges determine the final conversion.

Make the requested-versus-measured plot

Open Velocity Settings in Motion Studio. Use one graph channel for Motor 1 Setpoint and another for Motor 1 iSpeed, following the manufacturer's graphing guide. The selected screen gives the setpoint its meaning; here it is speed. The ordinary Speed trace is averaged, while iSpeed reports instantaneous encoder speed, so record which signal you use.

  1. Keep channel 2 at zero. Clear the graph, select a small slider range, and show a brief zero → low speed → zero sequence for channel 1 with the wheel supported.
  2. Scale the traces so their numeric axes are readable. Compare requested and measured values using those axes; independently scaled lines can appear to overlap even when their values differ.
  3. Save a screenshot containing the channel names, scale, and return to zero. Use Save CSV, documented in the Velocity Settings reference, to save the original data as runs/drive-left-original.csv. Record the software version, units, and signal names beside it; preserve the exported headers.
  4. Open the CSV and identify its time and channel columns before making an XY plot. If your installed version lacks export or an explicit timebase, keep the labelled screenshot as this checkpoint; do not invent timestamps. Repeat separately for channel 2 and save a second result.

The documented display update is 100 ms, so this view cannot establish sub-sample response time. Identify a visible overshoot, persistent oscillation, steady offset, or clean return to zero; report only what the recorded resolution supports. This procedure uses the existing controller graph and does not require a new plotting program.

Run the same experiment on each wheel. A wheel that reports the right speed in the air may still stall when loaded. On the floor, begin in a clear bounded area with stair access physically blocked and the disconnect within reach. Keep pets and children outside this initial test area. Start and stop gently; a polished floor makes traction another variable to measure.

Done: both wheels follow small requests without sustained oscillation, return to zero, and operate within your recorded motor/current limits. Save the plot and the controller configuration. A failure here belongs to the drivetrain; do not try to hide it by adjusting SLAM.

Setup gate · Prepare the robot computer before the ROS bridge

One or more setup blocks · Native Ubuntu 24.04 · Result: two ordinary ROS programs exchange messages

The remaining controller work uses ROS, so establish its environment here. On the selected robot computer, use native Ubuntu 24.04 and follow the official Jazzy Ubuntu installation through its Desktop Install option. The official source version is a fallback if that page does not render. This is the Ubuntu shell, outside the model-training virtual environment.

After completing the repository and package instructions, run these commands in terminal A. The first two create a local project folder on the Ubuntu computer and enter it:

mkdir -p ~/home-rover/notes ~/home-rover/runs
cd ~/home-rover
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-tf2-tools
ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker

In a second Ubuntu terminal, run:

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener

The expected result is a publishing message in A and corresponding received messages in B. Stop both with Ctrl+C. Save the Ubuntu release, ROS distribution and package versions in your project notes. Keep motor outputs disabled during software setup.

If the demo fails: first check that both terminals sourced the same Jazzy installation. If a demo package is missing, return to the Desktop Install step. Diagnose this local software exchange before adding USB devices, networking, or a controller driver.

Done: the local example exchanges messages. Continue directly to the bounded controller interface below; Chapter 05 reuses this installation.

Session · Give the rover a bounded software interface

Several integration sessions · Ubuntu robot computer · Output: manual movement with measured feedback and tested timeouts

The robot computer converts a body velocity request into two wheel speeds and publishes measurements back. Use the manufacturer's ROS 2 driver as an integration candidate, with its Python library available for smaller interface experiments. Pin the source revision you inspect. The documentation's example dimensions, commands, and installer defaults are not this robot's configuration; review them before use on the Jazzy system.

First establish a read-only connection: query firmware and encoder counts with motor commands disabled. Confirm your serial device by its identity, not by assuming it will always be /dev/ttyACM0. Then configure measured wheel radius, track width, count convention, signs, current limits, and maximum velocity. Keep the first linear speed cap at 0.10 m/s and initial trials at 0.05 m/s. These are conservative starting limits for evaluation, not proven safe speeds for every floor or collision.

Interface contractEvidence required before navigation
Fresh body commandOnly forward velocity and yaw rate are accepted for this base. Reject non-finite values, clamp limits, and expire the request after 0.25 s without a fresh operator command.
Controller communicationSet a 0.5 s serial timeout, save it, power-cycle, and read it back. Keep host-command expiry separate: continuing encoder queries must not preserve an old velocity request.
Measured stateRead encoder differences with timestamps; handle wraparound and controller reset explicitly. Invalid reads or reset trigger a stop and a logged fault, not a fabricated distance.
ROS integrationMatch the installed navigation stack's actual command type, including Twist versus TwistStamped. Publish wheel-derived odometry and exactly one odom→base_link transform owner. Chapter 06 develops the geometry.
Restart behaviourStart disarmed at zero. After a reset, communication fault, or physical stop, require a deliberate re-arm and a fresh operator command. Reconnecting alone or receiving an old stream does not restore motion.

The controller settings reference documents the communication timeout. Treat the specified 0.25/0.5 s values as initial design settings and verify their behaviour on your installed firmware and driver. A delayed process or an unhealthy connection is part of the experiment, not something we assume away.

Ask your coding agent to inspect the pinned driver's implementation against this table and implement only missing behaviour. Have it identify where command age is checked, where a failed encoder read is handled, and where zero is sent. You should be able to trace one request from input to wheel command and one measurement back to odometry before accepting the change.

Done: first with wheels suspended, stop the velocity publisher while encoder polling continues; then kill the bridge process; then disconnect its network input. Test the physical disconnect separately. Record whether and when motion ceases in every case. Repeat on the bounded floor at the initial speed and record stopping distance. Resolve any continued or resumed movement before attaching navigation.

When the first movement disagrees with your prediction

SymptomNext diagnostic
No encoder movementCheck encoder supply/reference and channel assignments with power removed before changing wiring. Verify a hand turn changes the expected channel.
Wheel accelerates in velocity modeDisconnect motor power. Recheck command/encoder signs and count units with low-duty open-loop tests.
Computer resets when motors startMeasure power under load, inspect the separated supply paths and USB grounding, and check startup demand. More training data cannot fix a voltage drop.
Robot curves while both speed plots agreeInspect rolling wheel diameter, tyre slip, caster drag, and load distribution. Equal angular speed does not guarantee equal ground travel.
Robot continues after the operator stopsTest host command expiry while status polling remains active. Then test the independent controller timeout by terminating communication entirely.

The first movement is yours

Keep a short video of manual forward movement, a turn, and a stop, plus the direction/count/current/timeout log. The robot now has a physical behaviour you can inspect. Next, connect and inspect its sensors so one trip can support mapping, model evaluation, and later reconstruction.

05 · Sensors and evidence

Give the rover
eyes and a rangefinder.

Inspect each sensor now. The next chapter establishes its geometry, and Chapter 07 records a run you can replay.

The rover is manually controllable and passes its stopping checks. Now we add observations. The reference mapping route uses a horizontal 2D lidar and wheel encoders. Camera images supply our learning task; calibrated depth becomes useful when we reconstruct surfaces in three dimensions. These observations share a clock and a set of coordinate frames so we can later ask what was seen from a particular position.

A ROS topic is a named stream of messages. A driver translates a device’s interface into those messages. The names below are our course contract; the manufacturer’s driver may use different defaults. We will inspect the actual names and remap them deliberately. Copying a topic name into a command does not make a sensor publish it.

Give each computer a clear job

MachineDefault roleWhat we check
Windows 11 / RTX 4090Fusion, Bambu Studio, editor, controller setup, image collection and trainingChapter 03 starts with a working CPU environment. GPU support is an optional separate environment check.
Native Ubuntu 24.04 x86 computer on roverUSB sensor I/O, ROS 2 Jazzy, local command expiration, recording and initial mapping/navigationExact computer supply, thermal limits, USB bandwidth, drivers and software revisions before mounting.
GB10 Spark on LANOptional later training, reconstruction or model servingArm64 software/container compatibility and the selected framework’s support for its GPU. An x86 environment cannot simply be copied across.

The onboard computer can be modest because the expensive experiments can run from recordings. It still needs to acquire messages and enforce the local command contract while the network is absent. We are choosing this arrangement to keep the first sensor and control connections on one native Linux machine.

WSL2 remains useful for Linux tools and offline work on Windows. Microsoft documents its networking modes, and USB access has a separate setup. For live robotics, check discovery, firewall rules, USB forwarding and timestamps explicitly. Keep the first live recording on the rover computer. The Spark hardware guide identifies its Arm architecture; it does not establish compatibility for every robotics package.

Session 05A · See one sensor before integrating three

45–60 minutes per device · Ubuntu computer, lidar, camera as available · Result: inspectable sensor messages

  1. Keep motor outputs disabled. Reuse the Jazzy installation verified at the Chapter 04 robot-computer setup gate. If you are starting with a bench sensor before finishing the chassis, complete that setup gate first, then return here. Record the sensor driver repository and commit or package versions.
  2. Install the selected lidar’s manufacturer driver. The reference candidate is the RPLIDAR A1 with Slamtec’s ROS 2 driver. Match the launch file and serial settings to the exact device. Inspect the scan in RViz; hold a flat object at a tape-measured distance and identify its returns.
  3. For a camera already on hand, first obtain a stable image using its own viewer and save stills for the model. The later RGB-D candidate is a RealSense D435i; verify its firmware, SDK, ROS wrapper and USB support together before committing to it. Use the manufacturer’s ROS wrapper as the integration reference. A colour image alone does not supply depth.
  4. Inspect the topic names and message types, then write a launch configuration that remaps the streams to the contract below. Leave optional depth absent until it actually works. Save device serial numbers so a second camera cannot silently become the first.
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 topic list -t
ros2 topic info /scan --verbose
ros2 topic echo /scan --once
ros2 topic hz /scan

These inspection commands run after a driver publishes /scan. Stop the rate display with Ctrl+C. Its observed rate depends on the device and the machine; compare it with the configured sensor mode. A blank RViz view can come from a missing transform or unsuitable fixed frame even when messages exist.

See the first scan before the complete transform tree exists

  1. Keep the lidar stationary. In the single /scan message printed above, find header.frame_id and copy its exact value. This names the coordinates in which its ranges were measured.
  2. Run ros2 run rviz2 rviz2 in a terminal with Jazzy sourced. In Global Options → Fixed Frame, enter that actual laser-frame name. We deliberately use the sensor's own frame for this first inspection; no map frame is needed yet.
  3. Click Add → By topic, choose /scan with the LaserScan display, and confirm the display status. If it reports an incompatible QoS policy, compare the publisher details from ros2 topic info /scan --verbose with the display's reliability setting.
  4. Place the cardboard target in the scan plane, then move it a measured distance. Inspect the corresponding returns. A stationary sensor-frame view checks these readings; it does not establish a room map or robot localization.
  5. Save the RViz configuration as ~/home-rover/notes/lidar-bench.rviz and a screenshot with the frame and topic visible. Chapter 06 will connect this frame to the rover.

The official RViz guide explains displays and fixed frames. If messages arrive but the view remains blank, inspect the display's status before changing the driver.

Done: you can point to one real measurement, its units, timestamp and frame, and explain how it relates to the object you moved.

The recording contract

TopicMessage / purposeReadiness check
/scansensor_msgs/LaserScan; horizontal rangesDistance units, scan orientation, timestamps and actual laser frame match the mount.
/odomnav_msgs/Odometry; measured wheel-motion estimateParent is odom, child is base_link; velocity/pose signs pass the next chapter’s checks.
/tfDynamic frame transformsThe raw acquisition run contains odom → base_link, with no SLAM or localization publisher of map → odom.
/tf_staticFixed sensor mounting transformsMeasured base_link → laser and camera mounting/optical transforms are present with one authoritative publisher per edge.
/rgb/image, /rgb/camera_infoColour image and its camera calibrationCorrect resolution, encoding, calibration and optical frame; names explicitly remapped from the driver.
/depth/image, /depth/camera_infoOptional calibrated depth streamDepth units and alignment convention recorded. Invalid depth is unknown, never a zero-distance surface.

Chapter 06 teaches the frame geometry. You can bench-check each sensor now, but complete those frame and odometry checks in Chapter 06, then follow Chapter 07 to record the room. The order is connect → check geometry → record → map.

Move the learning experiment onto the rover

Your first model learned from hand-held images. A low camera sees different proportions, shadows and occlusion. Collect a new, named capture session from the mounted camera and label both target-present and target-absent images. Treat it as a stress test of the frozen model first. If it exposes a gap, create a new development dataset and reserve new final-test sessions. Do not quietly fold the old test images into training and keep reporting the old score.

The supplied learning program accepts ordinary image files. Exporting timestamped images from a bag and matching them to poses is a later integration task; Chapter 09 defines the evidence format. Keep an observation’s capture position distinct from the object’s position.

Next: make the coordinate frames and wheel measurements agree →

06 · Geometry you can inspect

Give the room coordinates.

A camera sees a chair. An encoder sees a wheel turn. We need a shared account of where those observations came from before they can describe your room.

Put the rover beside a wall and move it sideways by hand. The wall stayed still, but its position relative to the rover changed. That distinction is the beginning of mapping: a measurement has meaning relative to a named coordinate system, at a particular time. In this chapter, we will make those relationships visible and check them against a ruler.

We use ROS 2 Jazzy on the rover’s native Ubuntu 24.04 computer. ROS carries timestamped messages between programs; tf2 maintains the relationships between coordinate systems, called frames. The Windows workstation can display and analyze recordings. You can move suitable workloads to the Spark later, after the same recording works on the reference host.

Start here: complete the sensor inspection in Chapter 05A. This chapter expects a working sensor driver and the encoder bridge described in Chapter 04. The book does not bundle that hardware-specific bridge.
