If it is still being implemented, you can complete the paper geometry and depth-image exercises, then return to the bridge’s first failing acceptance check.

Session 06A · Put arrows on the robot

45–60 minutes · Tape, ruler, robot and frame sketch · Result: a measured coordinate diagram

We will use base_link as the rover’s body frame. Place its origin halfway between the drive-wheel contact points on the nominal flat floor, directly below the axle midpoint. This is a fixed point relative to the body: the axle is one effective rolling radius above it. Mark the origin’s vertical projection on the deck. Our planar wheel-odometry equations estimate the motion of this midpoint, so the published pose and the physical reference agree. Following ROS coordinate conventions, x points forward, y points left, and z points up. Distances in ROS are metres and angles are radians. Keep millimetres in your Fusion design, then convert them explicitly when entering robot geometry.

  1. Mark the origin’s projection and forward direction on the deck. Draw the left and right wheel centres, lidar centre, and camera mounting reference on one sheet.
  2. Measure each sensor’s offset from the origin. Write both the number and its unit: a mount 120 mm forward becomes x = 0.120 m. Measure sensor height from the nominal floor plane, along z. Include orientation; an offset alone cannot describe a tilted camera.
  3. Save those measurements with the CAD revision and a photograph. Moving the camera bracket later changes the calibration, even if the software stays identical.
  4. Draw this chain: map → odom → base_link → sensor frames. Label the program responsible for each connection.
FrameWhat you use it forWho supplies its relationship
base_linkA point fixed to the robot bodyThe robot description defines its fixed sensor mounts.
odomSmooth short-term motion, which gradually accumulates errorThe encoder/odometry bridge publishes odom → base_link.
mapThe room reference, corrected when observations reveal driftSLAM supplies map → odom while mapping; a localizer supplies it during fixed-map navigation.

A loop-closure correction can move the robot’s estimated position in map while its odom motion remains continuous. This is why we keep both frames. Read the definitions of odom and map in REP 105, then explain which one you would use to inspect a sudden correction to the room map.

Check: point to the origin’s projection, explain where it lies vertically, and explain every arrow in your sketch. At this stage, having no map frame is expected; mapping creates it in Chapter 07. If a sensor orientation is uncertain, inspect its manufacturer’s frame diagram before entering a rotation.

Next: turn wheel counts into a short motion estimate →

Session 06B · Ask the wheels how far they went

45–60 minutes · Encoder logs, tape measure and clear floor · Result: a sign-and-scale check

Odometry estimates movement from measured motion. For our differential-drive rover, the inputs are the rotation of its left and right wheels. A motor command is an instruction; encoder counts are measurements of rotation. Neither establishes exactly how far the robot travelled when a wheel slips.

Use the count convention verified in Chapter 04. The proposed Pololu motor has a nominal 48 counts per motor revolution and a 46.85:1 reduction, giving approximately 2249 counts per output revolution under that stated counting convention. A controller that counts different edges changes the number you should use. Confirm it by turning the output through a known rotation and inspecting the reported counts; do not fix a fourfold error by “calibrating” the wheel diameter.

For each short update, let dL and dR be the left and right ground-travel estimates. With effective rolling radius r, counts per output revolution N, and wheel-centre separation b:

dL = 2π × rL × change_in_left_counts / NL
dR = 2π × rR × change_in_right_counts / NR
forward_step = (dL + dR) / 2
heading_change = (dR - dL) / b

These equations describe an ideal rolling model. For an illustrative step with dL = 0.10 m, dR = 0.12 m, and b = 0.20 m, the midpoint advances about 0.11 m and turns left by 0.10 rad, about 5.7°. A small-step integrator uses the heading halfway through that turn when updating x and y. The physical test tells us where the idealization stops matching the rover.

  1. With motor outputs disabled and commands inhibited, keep the controller and encoder electronics powered, roll the robot forward slowly, and log both counts. USB alone does not power the RoboClaw controller and encoders. After the bridge’s sign convention is applied, both distances should increase. Turning the chassis left should produce a positive yaw change.
  2. Mark a straight, unobstructed baseline and measure it. Drive slowly along it under manual control. Compare tape distance with the odometry distance, noting any curve or wheel slip.
  3. Repeat the run before changing a parameter. A repeatable scale error suggests the count convention or rolling radius. An inconsistent error suggests traction, loose hardware, missed counts, or measurement technique.
  4. Make a slow turn and compare the direction and approximate angle with floor marks. Only tune effective track width after straight-line signs and scale are credible.

Check: save raw counts, configured counts/revolution, wheel dimensions, tape distance, odometry distance, and observed turn direction. A consistent short-run estimate is enough to proceed to sensor fusion; there is no promise that wheel-only odometry will stay aligned around the room.

Next: inspect what a distance sensor actually observed →

Session 06C · A return is evidence; a blank is a question

45–60 minutes · Live stationary lidar and optional depth images · Result: an annotated observation

The main mapping path uses a horizontal 2D lidar. Each valid return describes a range along a ray in the sensor’s scan plane. A tabletop above that plane and a small toy below it can both escape that slice. This is useful geometry for a first room map, with a specific field of view and specific blind spots.

  1. Inspect a stationary scan in RViz. Place a broad cardboard target in the scan plane and move it a measured distance. Compare the change in the displayed return.
  2. Identify a real wall, an object edge, and an area hidden behind an object. Label the drawing observed surface, observed free ray, or unknown.
  3. Lift a target out of the scan plane. Observe that its disappearance does not mean the whole volume is empty. Keep the initial test area clear of low objects and physically isolated from stairs.

Optional RGB-D adds a colour image and depth measurements. A point cloud is a collection of 3D samples produced from those measurements. For a calibrated, rectified image whose depth value Z is forward distance, a pixel (u, v) becomes a camera-frame point:

X = (u - cx) × Z / fx
Y = (v - cy) × Z / fy
Z = depth_in_metres

The calibration supplies the focal lengths fx, fy and image centre cx, cy. At Z = 2 m, a pixel 60 pixels to the right of centre with fx = 600 pixels lies 0.20 m right of the optical axis. This is an illustrative calculation, not a measurement from your camera. Invalid depth stays invalid; a zero depth value must not become an obstacle at the camera origin.

Check the driver’s image encoding and depth scale before converting values. Also check whether depth is registered to the colour image. Colour and depth pixels from different viewpoints cannot be paired merely because their arrays have the same shape. Camera optical frames conventionally point z forward, x right, and y down; the driver’s transforms connect that convention to the robot body.

Check: explain why an unseen patch behind a chair remains unknown. If you have RGB-D data, save one colour image, its matching depth image and calibration, with a marked pixel whose computed distance you can plausibly check. If the camera has not arrived, finish the lidar exercise and continue.

Next: check the live frame chain before asking SLAM to use it →

Session 06D · Make the frame chain tell the truth

45–60 minutes · Running acquisition stack · Result: a frame diagram and a checked live frame chain

Run these inspection commands in the sourced Jazzy environment. They do not create the robot bridge or sensor drivers; those programs must already be publishing their measured data.

ros2 topic list -t
ros2 topic echo /odom --once
ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo odom base_link
ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames

Inspect the generated frame diagram using the Nav2 transform guide as a reference. Each child frame needs one parent and one authoritative publisher for that connection. The camera driver may supply its own internal optical transforms; do not publish conflicting copies.

ObservationYour next diagnostic
The scan moves with the robot instead of staying on the wallInspect fixed sensor orientation and odom → base_link direction/signs.
A transform is unavailable at the image timestampCompare clock sources, synchronization, message timestamps, and transform history before increasing queues.
The robot appears hundreds of metres wideCheck millimetre-to-metre conversion in the robot description.
Frames flicker or jump between two positionsLook for competing publishers or simultaneous live and replay data.

Chapter checkpoint: the saved diagram matches your physical frame sketch, signs and scale pass the short tests, and live messages contain sensor data plus the required transforms. Keep the acquisition run free of a map → odom publisher so Chapter 07 can calculate that correction afresh.

Next: record a raw run and build your first measured room map →

07 · The first survey

Measure one room.

Drive once, replay the observations, and check whether the map agrees with the room you actually measured.

We now have two imperfect accounts of movement. Wheel odometry says how the rover probably moved; the lidar says how nearby surfaces appeared from successive positions. Simultaneous localization and mapping, or SLAM, uses their agreement to estimate a route and a map together. When the robot recognizes a place it has revisited, a loop closure can correct accumulated drift.

Our first deliverable is a metric 2D occupancy map: a grid with a known scale whose cells represent occupied, observed-free, and unknown space. It is a slice through your room at the lidar’s height. It can describe useful layout and distances, but it cannot establish ceiling height, all furniture surfaces, or whether a low toy is beneath the scan plane.

We will use SLAM Toolbox for this first map. The depth-camera reconstruction you are interested in remains a later use of the same recording habit. Getting one measured floor map now gives us a place to attach those experiments.

Before this chapter: pass the frame and odometry checks. Your live acquisition stack must publish /scan, /odom, /tf, and /tf_static. The first session records those streams with no map → odom publisher running. The recipes below use actual stock ROS tools, but their success depends on the hardware bridge, calibration, and recording you build. They have not been executed on your rover.

Session 07A · Plan and record the room

One or two 45–60 minute blocks after the frame gate · One bounded test area · Result: a recording and its manifest

Choose a bounded area on one floor, with stair access physically blocked. Keep children and pets outside the first test area and clear small objects from the route. We are measuring a mostly static room before asking the system to handle your household’s normal motion.

  1. Open notes/room-reference.md and the labelled sketch from Session 01A. Check them against the room as it is today. Mark the start, two or three visible wall faces, and a short manual route with a gentle loop back toward the start.
  2. Recheck the three reference spans R1–R3. Reuse a span only where the lidar can observe the same surfaces at its mounted height; otherwise revise the endpoints and label the change in your note. Keep three distinct spans with two directions represented. Record their actual lengths in metres, endpoints, and measurement height so a baseboard measurement does not silently become a wall-face comparison. Save the dated revision with this survey.
  3. Declare a first acceptance target before viewing the map. Use absolute error no greater than 0.10 m on each reference span as a provisional layout goal. This is a course target to test, not a sensor specification or a promise of achieved accuracy.
  1. Complete Chapter 06’s frame and wheel checks. Set live nodes to use_sim_time:=false. Ensure the clock is sane before acquisition; record on the same computer first. Separate computers require clock synchronization and latency checks.
  2. Start only the validated drivers, wheel bridge and transform publishers. Stop SLAM, localization and navigation. We want raw wheel and sensor observations without previously computed map corrections.
  3. Record a stationary segment, then drive a short slow loop and return near the start. Keep the same bounded area and have the physical stop within reach. Do not record motion command topics for later replay.
  4. Stop recording with Ctrl+C. Save the computer/software versions, sensor identities, mount revision, wheel parameters, scene notes and measured reference distances beside the bag.
# On the robot computer, after all four topics pass inspection:
mkdir -p ~/home-rover/data
cd ~/home-rover
ros2 bag record -o data/room_001 /scan /odom /tf /tf_static

# After stopping the recorder:
ros2 bag info data/room_001

This is the minimum lidar mapping recording. When the colour streams work, add /rgb/image /rgb/camera_info to a new recording command and output directory. Add the depth pair only after its calibration gate. Check storage and message counts with a short recording before attempting a whole room. The output directory must not already contain a previous bag.

Use the run-manifest template. Never describe illustrative values as measured calibration. Keep the raw recording unchanged and put derived maps, exported images and models in separate directories.

If a recorded stream is missing: inspect the publisher’s actual name, offered QoS and rate with ros2 topic info --verbose. Confirm the recorder discovered it and retained static transforms. Fix one stream, then repeat a short recording. Do not proceed because the directory has a plausible file size.

Done: one recording contains the planned route, its raw topics and transforms, with the reference measurements and manifest saved beside it. This same data/room_001 bag is the input to the next session.

Next: replay this recording into a map →

Session 07B · Replay the room without moving the robot

45–60 minutes · Ubuntu/Jazzy analysis environment · Result: one inspectable map

Recordings separate data collection from debugging. With motor power off and robot command processes stopped, you can compare mapping settings against the same observations. Use a separate ROS domain for the replay terminals, and keep live sensor and transform publishers out of that domain. These commands run in an Ubuntu shell; they are not PowerShell commands.

After following the official Jazzy installation, install the mapping tools. Create your project folders and copy the configuration supplied by your installed package:

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-slam-toolbox ros-jazzy-nav2-map-server
mkdir -p ~/home-rover/config ~/home-rover/maps
cp "$(ros2 pkg prefix --share slam_toolbox)/config/mapper_params_online_async.yaml" \
  ~/home-rover/config/slam.yaml

Edit config/slam.yaml. Keep the installed solver settings initially. Set base_frame: base_link, odom_frame: odom, map_frame: map, scan_topic: /scan, and mode: mapping for our frame contract. Start with resolution: 0.05, a five-centimetre cell. Check the configured valid laser ranges against the actual driver and room; reject invalid measurements rather than inventing returns.

The upstream Jazzy example configuration uses base_footprint. Copying it unchanged would ask for a frame our current robot contract does not provide. This is the kind of small integration mismatch we want to catch before interpreting a poor map as a failure of SLAM.

In terminal A, start the mapper. Domain 71 is an example analysis domain; use it in every terminal participating in this replay, with no hardware-control nodes attached.

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=71
ros2 launch slam_toolbox online_async_launch.py \
  slam_params_file:=$HOME/home-rover/config/slam.yaml \
  use_sim_time:=true

In terminal B, source the same environment, set the same domain, and play the raw bag. Here ~/home-rover/data/room_001 is your actual bag directory, including its metadata; this is the directory recorded in Session 07A above.

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=71
ros2 bag info ~/home-rover/data/room_001
ros2 bag play ~/home-rover/data/room_001 --clock --rate 0.5 \
  --topics /scan /odom /tf /tf_static

Open RViz in the same domain with use_sim_time set to true, set its fixed frame to map, and display the map, scan, and robot frames. The --clock option supplies playback time; every consumer of the replay must use that time. For a later live mapping session, use use_sim_time:=false and the synchronized live timestamps instead.

Check: surfaces appear in a consistent place as the rover moves, and the route roughly agrees with your sketch. If nothing appears, inspect topic names, frame availability, and clock settings before tuning scan matching. If a wall doubles during turns, revisit odometry, sensor pose, timing, and wheel slip.

A replay trap: /tf contains many frame edges in one topic. Selecting that topic does not remove an old map → odom edge. If your bag was recorded while SLAM was running, collect a clean raw bag or explicitly filter the derived edge before recomputing SLAM. Do not let old and new mapping corrections compete.

Next: measure the map rather than judging its appearance →

Session 07C · Put numbers beside the picture

45–60 minutes · Map, reference sketch and measurement log · Result: an accuracy report

A map can look plausible while being stretched, duplicated, or consistently displaced. Measure the same three spans you recorded before the run. If you inspect raster pixels, use the map’s saved resolution; if you inspect points in RViz, use their map-frame coordinates. Record which wall boundaries you selected.

ReferencePhysical distanceMap distanceSigned error
Illustrative wall span A3.04 m3.00 m−0.04 m
Your span BMeasureMeasureMap − physical
Your span CMeasureMeasureMap − physical

The example row demonstrates the calculation; it is not a result from this project. A 0.05 m grid resolution means cells are five centimetres wide. It does not establish five-centimetre accuracy. Range noise, pose errors, wall thickness in the raster, and how you chose the endpoints all influence the comparison.

  1. Compute the error for each span and compare its absolute value with the declared target.
  2. Inspect the route near the loop closure. A correction may improve alignment, but a false match can also fold the map. Check the room shape against your physical sketch.
  3. Collect a second independent survey and repeat the measurements. Agreement across runs is evidence of repeatability; agreement with tape measurements is evidence about accuracy.
  4. If a span fails, change one justified cause, then rerun the same recording before collecting another. Record which change helped and which problem remained.

Check: you can show the map, three measured comparisons, and the result of a second run. A failed target becomes a specific debugging question. It does not require starting a new robot or completing an entire SLAM textbook.

Next: save the map and its provenance for navigation →

Session 07D · Save the map you can explain

30–60 minutes · Running mapper and project folder · Result: a versioned map package

While /map is available in the replay domain, save the occupancy grid for the next chapter. Use the same sourced environment, domain, and replay clock setting:

ros2 run nav2_map_server map_saver_cli \
  -f $HOME/home-rover/maps/room_001 \
  --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true

Keep the resulting YAML and image together. The YAML supplies scale, origin, and occupancy interpretation. For live mapping, use use_sim_time:=false. A saved image without its metadata is a picture, not a complete navigation map.

Also serialize the SLAM Toolbox pose graph using its save/serialization interface if you want to resume that mapping session. A pose graph retains scan-and-pose relationships; the raster grid used by AMCL does not. Save the raw bag regardless, because it lets you rebuild results with changed software.

Put the bag identifier, software/package versions, copied configuration, reference measurements, room sketch, and a frame diagram beside the saved map. Give this collection a map_revision. Later observations will refer to that revision so a room-map correction does not silently change the meaning of an old location.

Chapter checkpoint: you have a saved metric room map with its metadata, a measurement report, and a raw run that can reproduce it. Your claim is now specific: “this map passed these checks in this room.”

Next: use the saved map to reach one selected destination →

08 · The first autonomous trip

Choose a destination.

Turn a point on your room map into a short, supervised journey—with evidence that the robot can stop and recognize when the trip has failed.

You already know how to drive the rover. This chapter changes who chooses the wheel commands: you choose a destination, and a navigation system selects the route and local motion. We will use Nav2, the ROS 2 navigation framework, while keeping the first trip short enough to understand from end to end.

Three jobs have to cooperate. Localization estimates where the rover is in your saved map. A planner proposes a route through available space. A controller turns the route into short-term velocity requests while current sensor observations influence which movements are acceptable. The motor controller still performs its local wheel-speed control; the navigation planner does not replace that loop.

We begin with a fixed map and AMCL, a lidar-based localizer. Stop SLAM before starting this setup so only AMCL owns map → odom. Local obstacle observations can change the space available for this trip without continually rewriting the underlying room map.

Integration status: this is a build-and-verification plan for your custom rover. The official packages supply navigation algorithms; your measured robot description, controller integration, command routing, and Nav2 configuration must be completed and checked. No physical waypoint run or stopping distance has been demonstrated by this book. Use the Jazzy first-robot setup guide alongside the bounded tasks below.

Session 08A · Make the robot contract explicit

One or more 45–60 minute blocks · Native Ubuntu host, saved map and measured rover · Result: a configuration you can review

Installing Nav2 does not connect it to a motor. Before enabling movement, write down the route from its final velocity output to the motor controller. There must be one selected command source at a time: manual control or navigation. A second teleoperation publisher left running can make a perfectly reasonable planner appear erratic.

  1. Open the robot description and compare its sensor offsets with the current physical mounts. Confirm live /scan, /odom, fixed sensor transforms, and odom → base_link.
  2. Repeat the manual stop and command-timeout tests from Chapter 04. Recheck at the intended battery state and load; additional sensors change both mass and wiring.
  3. Install the Jazzy navigation packages, then copy the configuration supplied with the installed nav2_bringup package into your project.
  4. Adapt that copy using the table below. Record the package versions and chosen controller plugin with the file.
  5. Have your coding agent review the file against the measured robot contract. You should be able to point to each parameter that controls geometry, speed, observations, and command type.
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-navigation2 ros-jazzy-nav2-bringup
cp "$(ros2 pkg prefix --share nav2_bringup)/params/nav2_params.yaml" \
  ~/home-rover/config/nav2.yaml
Configuration areaSet it from this evidence
Frame namesOur contract uses map, odom, and base_link. Check AMCL’s base frame as well as both costmaps and the navigator.
Robot footprintMeasure the occupied outline around the actual body-frame origin, including wheels, brackets, and protruding cables. Configure both local and global costmaps.
Obstacle observationsUse the actual /scan topic, frame, valid range, and message type. Check marking and clearing behavior in the local costmap.
Motion limitsStart at the manually demonstrated 0.05 m/s; keep the initial hard cap at 0.10 m/s. Match controller, velocity-smoother, and bridge limits. Use measured conservative acceleration and turn limits.
Command routeFollow the final output through any smoother or collision monitor to the bridge. Match Twist versus TwistStamped explicitly. Intermediate outputs must not also reach the wheels.
Failure behaviorStop on lost commands, stale required observations, operator cancellation, or controller fault. Identify the local process that enforces each condition.

The installed sample is a starting reference, not a calibrated robot configuration. Plugin choices and available parameters can change between package releases. Inspect ros2 launch nav2_bringup bringup_launch.py --show-args and the documentation matching the installed version before using a copied example.

For footprint setup, work through Nav2’s footprint guide and visualize the resulting outline. A robot that fits at rest can still sweep a corner into an obstacle while turning. A horizontal lidar also cannot rule out an overhead obstruction or a drop-off. The first test zone therefore has known clearance and physically blocked stair access.

Check: every row has a measured value or a named, tested implementation. If the bridge or freshness guard is unfinished, the next task is that specific integration—not an autonomous trial. You can continue the model-training track while completing it.

Next: place the stationary robot correctly in the saved map →

Session 08B · Convince yourself the robot knows where it is

45–60 minutes · Live sensors, motor outputs disabled initially · Result: a localized robot and sensible costmaps

Return to the live ROS domain used by the rover; the isolated replay domain from Chapter 07 is not the live system. Stop all bag playback and SLAM processes. Start the verified live acquisition and odometry stack, then start Nav2 with your reviewed files. This command assumes those files actually exist and the configuration gate above has passed.

ros2 launch nav2_bringup bringup_launch.py \
  map:=$HOME/home-rover/maps/room_001.yaml \
  params_file:=$HOME/home-rover/config/nav2.yaml \
  slam:=false use_localization:=true use_sim_time:=false

In RViz, display the saved map, laser scan, robot footprint, local costmap, and global costmap. Use 2D Pose Estimate to give AMCL an approximate starting position and heading that agree with the physical placement. The localizer refines that hypothesis from sensor observations; it does not know which room you placed the robot in merely because it loaded a map.

  1. With the rover stationary, inspect whether visible wall returns align with the saved walls. Check the robot heading against the room sketch.
  2. Verify that map → odom has one owner and that odometry continues to update. An apparently good single frame does not prove ongoing localization.
  3. Place a broad test obstacle in the scan plane and watch it appear in the local costmap. Remove it and observe whether later valid rays clear the space as configured.
  4. Inspect unknown areas and the inflated clearance around obstacles. Confirm that the first planned route will stay within surveyed, physically inspected space.

A costmap represents navigation preference and obstruction around the robot. Inflation raises the cost near obstacles so paths can leave clearance. Its margin must account for the measured body, localization uncertainty, and stopping behavior; shrinking it until a route appears is not evidence that the robot fits.

Check: the rover’s displayed placement agrees with its real placement, the footprint contains its physical outline, and the test obstacle appears and clears as expected. If walls do not align, diagnose initialization, map revision, frames, and scan timing before changing planner settings.

Next: make one short trip with a clear stopping point →

Session 08C · Go half a metre, then stop

45–60 minutes · Clear supervised floor area · Result: a recorded waypoint trial

Choose a destination about half a metre ahead in known free space. Mark it physically so the success claim does not depend entirely on the map display. Begin with the same low speed already demonstrated under manual control. Keep the operator stop within reach and the initial route clear of people and animals.

  1. Review the planned path in RViz before enabling the motor output. Check the entire swept footprint, not only the line through its centre.
  2. Enable the verified command route and submit the goal. Observe the robot, the reported navigation status, and whether its estimated position follows its physical movement.
  3. At the end, measure the physical final position relative to the mark. Record goal tolerance, final error, elapsed time, and any manual intervention. Use a provisional 0.15 m position target for these first short trips; the test establishes whether it is realistic.
  4. Repeat from the same marked start. Keep unsuccessful attempts in the log. A success message without plausible physical position and stopped wheels does not pass the trial.

Hold automatic recovery behaviors to the same visibility and clearance requirements. A default recovery can spin or reverse the robot. Configure the initial behavior tree and motion limits so it cannot perform an untested maneuver merely because the forward route failed. A cleanly reported aborted goal is useful evidence.

Check: save three trial records, including outcome, endpoint error, and interventions. Proceed when the short route behaves repeatably and stopping is dependable. If it oscillates near the goal, inspect minimum controllable speed, odometry, goal tolerances, and controller limits in that order.

Next: change the room and test the failure paths →

Session 08D · Give the robot a reason to refuse

45–60 minutes · Same route and a broad test obstacle · Result: an honest navigation envelope

Your home changes. The first useful response to a change is often to stop or decline a route. Recognizing the obstacle as “laundry” can come later; geometric observations already provide a reason not to drive through it.

  1. Place the test obstacle on the planned route before starting. Choose a target tall enough to intersect the scan plane. Confirm that the costmap sees it, then request the trip. Accept a clearance-respecting alternate route or an explicit refusal.
  2. Cancel a short trip and verify that the rover stops. Record the observed delay and travel after cancellation.
  3. In a controlled low-speed test, interrupt fresh motion commands. Confirm that the local motor timeout stops the rover without depending on the Windows workstation or Spark responding.
  4. With motor output disabled first, interrupt the required sensor stream and verify the freshness guard inhibits motion. Re-enable only after the failure behavior is demonstrated. A velocity publisher that keeps repeating commands can hide a failed sensor.
  5. Restore the normal configuration and repeat the uncomplicated trip. Save both the failure test and recovery procedure.

Record the boundaries of what passed: floor surface, load, speed, sensor coverage, lighting where relevant, room/map revision, and failure handling. A scan-plane obstacle test does not establish detection of shoelaces, low toys, transparent surfaces, or stair edges. Those become separate experiments when you expand the operating area.

Chapter checkpoint: the rover can make a short supervised trip on the measured map, avoid or refuse a visible blocked route, and stop under the tested cancellation and timeout conditions. You have evidence for a bounded navigation capability rather than a claim of general household autonomy.

Next: connect your trained model’s observations to places on this map →

Chapter 09 · Connect the two tracks

Give observations
a place and time

Your model has an opinion. Your map has coordinates. We will connect them without inventing facts between the two.

Suppose the robot's camera recognizes your chosen toy. The useful first answer is: “This image looked like the toy, from this viewpoint, at this time.” That is already more informative than a label floating over a video stream. It lets you inspect the source image, return to the observation area, and decide whether the evidence still matters.

A whole-image classifier cannot tell you which pixel contains the toy or how far away it is. In this chapter we store the robot's observation location and leave the object's location unknown. That distinction gives us an honest first spatial memory and a clear reason to add segmentation and depth later.

What runs now: the downloadable memory exercise uses Python's standard library and illustrative records. It runs on your Windows machine without ROS, a GPU, or a finished rover. Connecting live predictions to timestamped robot poses is a separate integration task described below. This memory never supplies collision decisions or motor commands.

Session 09A · Build a memory you can question

45–60 minutes · Python 3.10+ · Finish: explain exactly which observation supports an answer

Download memory.py, the illustrative observations, and the data contract into home-rover/memory/. Open PowerShell in home-rover, beside the Chapter 03 virtual environment. Reuse that interpreter; this exercise needs no additional packages. The image paths in the demo are placeholders; there are no corresponding household images or measured model results.

$LearnerPython = ".\.venv\Scripts\python.exe"
& $LearnerPython memory/memory.py import memory/demo.sqlite memory/observations-demo.jsonl
& $LearnerPython memory/memory.py recent memory/demo.sqlite --map-id room-a --map-revision v1 --target-id demo-toy --as-of 2026-10-27T19:20:00Z --max-age-minutes 60 --min-score 0.8

The importer should report three added observations. The query should return demo-01 as a historical candidate sighting and include the newer negative observation, demo-02, in its evidence list. The third row belongs to map revision v2, so it is excluded. A newer negative view does not prove the toy vanished: visibility, viewpoint, and classifier error can all change the answer.

  1. Inspect the candidate's timestamp, image reference, model identifier, and observer_pose. Confirm that object_position is null.
  2. Change the time window to ten minutes. At the stated replay time, both v1 rows are too old. An empty result means “no qualifying evidence,” not “no toy in the room.”
  3. Restore the sixty-minute window and change --min-score to 0.99. The candidate_sightings list becomes empty, while recent_observations still contains both v1 records. The score filter applies only to positive candidates; all recent evidence remains available for inspection.
  4. Query revision v2. Its coordinates belong to that map; comparing them directly with v1 would require a known transformation between the maps.
  5. Import the unchanged file again. Identical observations are retained once. Changing an existing record while keeping its ID produces an error; the original evidence remains intact.

Demo checkpoint: you can explain why an observation appears, why another is excluded, and why neither establishes a current object position. Keep the output beside the input file. This synthetic exercise prepares you for the real-record task below; it does not complete the robot’s spatial-memory milestone.

If the import fails: check that the input contains one complete JSON object per line and that timestamps include a timezone. Use the exact demo first. A map identifier, pose, and score are required because a label alone cannot support the spatial claim.

Keep evidence separate from interpretation

The observation template is a starting record for your own runs. Replace its example values; do not copy its zeros into a real recording. Store the image reference, capture timestamp, map revision, recording ID, model artifact identifier, target concept ID, label, score, and robot pose at capture time. The target concept ID separates classifiers for different things; it does not establish the identity of an individual physical object. A score of 0.9 is a model output, not an established 90% chance of correctness. Choose a display threshold using validation examples from Chapter 03.

Build the first records by hand before automating the join. The task below uses stationary, measured viewpoints so you can inspect each claim. A later timestamped adapter must preserve the original clocks and verify their relationship before joining streams. A pose from “when inference finished” can be wrong if the rover moved while the model was running.

For a binary model, record the score for the chosen label. If its output is p(target_present) and the decision is absent, the corresponding score is 1 − p. Keep the classification threshold with the run configuration. For example, learn.py predict might return {"label":"absent","score_present":0.12}. Its memory record uses "label":"target_absent" and "score":0.88. A present decision with score 0.92 becomes "target_present" with score 0.92. These numbers illustrate the conversion, not measured predictions. The memory query’s 0.8 filter is illustrative and applies only to candidate_sightings; recent_observations retains the matching evidence regardless of label or score. Neither output calibrates the classifier.

Many frames of the same object are correlated observations. Counting twenty adjacent positive frames as twenty independent confirmations overstates your evidence. Later object tracking will associate views with a persistent object hypothesis; it will still need to handle two similar toys, occlusion, movement, and conflicting observations. Preserve source records so a changed interpretation can be traced backward.

Session 09B · Give five real observations a place

One or more 45–60 minute blocks · Your saved model, mounted camera and checked map · Finish: import and inspect five real records

We now connect the parts you built. The synthetic database stays in memory/demo.sqlite. Your real records go in a separate file and database, so illustrative coordinates cannot quietly become household evidence. Use your current map revision and the same target object that trained the classifier.

  1. Mark two stationary rover poses in your bounded test area. Establish their x_m, y_m and yaw_rad in the current map frame using measured offsets from mapped reference surfaces and a checked heading. Record the measured endpoints and uncertainty in your notes. The pose refers to the base_link origin established in Chapter 06, not the camera lens. If you cannot yet express the marked poses in that frame, finish the frame/map checks before proceeding.
  2. Keep the camera fixed to the rover, inhibit motor outputs, and place the rover at each marked pose. Capture five distinct images across the two poses, including target-present and target-absent scenes. Put them in memory/images/. Record each image’s actual capture time with its timezone and its marked pose. Keep the rover stationary during each capture; do not substitute the time when inference finishes. A verified timestamped map → base_link pose from your recording is also suitable once that association works.
  3. Run the saved classifier on each image using the command below, replacing the filename with an actual image. Keep its output even when it is wrong. Use the label/score conversion above and retain the model artifact identifier, classification threshold, target ID and source run.
  4. Copy the observation template into five complete records. Give each a unique ID, actual image path, actual capture timestamp, current map ID/revision, measured observer pose, and object_position: null. Add a pose_source note such as marked_pose_manual_measurement and a pose_uncertainty_note describing the method. The importer preserves these provenance notes. Save one JSON object per line as UTF-8 memory/observations-own.jsonl.
  5. Import and query the file. Set the query’s map, revision and target to match your records, and use an --as-of time at or just after their latest capture, with a window covering all five. Open every referenced image yourself, compare the model decision with what you see, and check the pose against the marked viewpoint or recording.
& $LearnerPython learn.py predict runs/cnn-7 memory/images/marked-01.jpg
(Get-FileHash runs/cnn-7/weights.pt -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
& $LearnerPython memory/memory.py import memory/own.sqlite memory/observations-own.jsonl

The hash command identifies the actual neural weights for model_id; keep run.json with them so the preprocessing and source revision remain traceable. For the query, reuse the demonstrated recent command with memory/own.sqlite and your real identifiers and time. The program stores image references but does not verify that a file exists or that a pose is accurate; your five-record inspection supplies that check.

Real-record checkpoint: five observations from your own images and saved model are imported, and the query returns all five in recent_observations for the chosen map, target and time window. Every image opens, every pose has a documented physical or timestamped basis, and every object position remains unknown. If no positive candidate survives the display threshold, report that outcome and inspect the model errors; do not change its decisions to make the result look successful.

If the robot/map is not ready: save the completed demo and continue the next incomplete mapping task. You can prepare images and model outputs now, but leave unmeasured poses out of the real database. An automatic ROS image-to-pose adapter remains future implementation work.

Session 09C · Calculate a location only when you have the measurements

45–60 minutes · Paper, calculator, recorded poses · Finish: transform a measured point and name the missing inputs for an image

Imagine a separately measured point lies 1.0 m forward and 0.2 m left of the robot base. The robot is at map position (2.0, 1.0) m, turned 90° counterclockwise from map +x. Rotating the point sends forward along map +y and left along map −x. Its map position is therefore (1.8, 2.0) m.

x_map = x_robot + cos(yaw) * forward - sin(yaw) * left
y_map = y_robot + sin(yaw) * forward + cos(yaw) * left

Predict the answer at zero yaw: (3.0, 1.2) m. Draw both cases before using the formula. This planar example assumes the point already exists in the base frame. An image pixel needs calibrated camera intrinsics and valid depth before it becomes a 3D point; that point then needs the camera-to-base and base-to-map transforms at capture time. ROS camera optical axes differ from the body axes, as specified in REP 103.

When you add a detector or segmenter, an image region can define which depth samples belong to a candidate object. Inspect the depth distribution and foreground/background mixing before storing a location estimate. A bounding-box center can hit the wall behind a hollow or partly occluded object. Store the localization method and uncertainty with the estimate; retain the image and measured points that produced it.

Done: your sketch and arithmetic agree, and you can distinguish an observer pose, a measured object point, and an image-only prediction. The starter intentionally rejects object coordinates until a different localization schema is designed.

Let language select a grounded task

A future request such as “show me where you last saw the toy” can retrieve candidate evidence and display its image, age, and observation location. Embeddings would help match flexible language to descriptions. They do not supply missing geometry, guarantee identity, or refresh stale observations. Begin with the exact labels in the database; add semantic retrieval when a real query exposes that limitation.

For a first movement request, use a small catalogue of already tested viewpoints: “go to the doorway view” resolves to a known waypoint. The language component proposes a named action. A deterministic adapter checks the action, map revision, allowed area, current localization, and navigation readiness. It then submits a goal to Nav2's NavigateToPose action, monitors feedback, and reports completion or failure. Keep arbitrary scripts, motor values, and automatic pushing outside this interface.

This adapter is a later implementation exercise, not bundled functionality. First test a text-to-JSON version that cannot move anything: valid waypoint, unknown name, ambiguous reference, stale map, and cancelled request. Preserve the local stop behavior from Chapter 04. A conversation should explain the outcome of a navigation task; it should not become the motor controller.

Done means this

Your offline memory returns inspectable evidence, excludes the wrong map revision, and keeps object location unknown for image-only predictions. You have imported and queried five real predictions from your own model, with source images and checked capture poses. The synthetic demonstration alone does not satisfy this checkpoint. Optional next: explore a 3D extension while keeping this working baseline →

Chapter 10 · A direction beyond the first room

Grow the room into
a research platform

Use the same recordings to investigate geometry, appearance, and meaning—one question at a time.

The first rover gives you a way to collect observations deliberately. Its next value comes from replaying those observations: you can improve a reconstruction, compare two models, or inspect a failed prediction while the chassis is switched off. Your Windows machine and RTX 4090 provide an experimental workspace; the Spark is another possible compute host once the selected software's ARM64 and accelerator support have been checked.

The default next branch is reconstruct a small, static patch of the room from recorded RGB-D data. It builds directly on calibration, timestamps, poses, and measurement checks. The other branches below stay available after that checkpoint. These are research plans with entry and exit conditions; they are not claims that the first build already supports them.

Give each representation a job

RepresentationWhat we ask itWhat it does not establish by itself
Occupancy grid or octreeWhich regions have evidence of occupancy or free space?Unobserved space is not automatically traversable.
TSDF and extracted surfaceWhere do repeated depth observations suggest surfaces?A surface reconstruction alone is not a complete free-space or navigation policy.
Gaussian splatsWhat would this scene look like from another viewpoint?Visual plausibility does not certify dimensions or collision clearance.
Semantic observations and object hypothesesWhat might this be, where was it observed, and what supports that claim?Labels and embeddings do not guarantee persistent identity or current truth.

Voxel carving is one way to update space along measured rays. The endpoint and the path leading to it contain different evidence; areas behind an occluder may remain unseen. OctoMap is a primary reference for probabilistic 3D occupancy with free, occupied, and unknown regions. Read its overview and sketch one ray hitting a chair. Mark what that ray tells you and what it leaves unknown.

Research session 10A · Reconstruct one corner

Several 45–60 minute sessions · Prerequisites: replayable RGB-D, calibration, valid camera poses · Finish: inspect a measured surface and its gaps

A truncated signed distance function, or TSDF, combines depth measurements around estimated surfaces. Repeated observations can reduce noise, while wrong poses can create duplicated walls. We will use that behavior as a diagnostic. Start with a static chair and wall corner; a child or pet crossing the scan creates another problem before we understand the first one.

  1. Save a copy of one short recording and its calibration. Verify depth units and the transform direction expected by the reconstruction tool. Keep the original unchanged.
  2. Follow Open3D's TSDF integration example on its documented example data in a separate environment. Its source documentation describes integration from depth images and known poses. Record the version that actually runs.
  3. Write a small converter for your own RGB-D frames, intrinsics, and poses. Inspect three transformed frames together before integrating the complete sequence. This converter depends on the selected camera and recording format and is not supplied by the Fieldbook.
  4. Choose a coarse voxel size for the first view, then compare one finer setting on the same input. Record runtime, memory use, gaps, and changes to a few measured spans. Smaller voxels do not repair bad calibration.
  5. Extract and save the surface. Compare it with physical measurements and inspect unseen areas. Keep the navigation map unchanged while evaluating this reconstruction.

Done: the saved result has a reproducible input manifest, a stated scale, several measurement comparisons, and labelled gaps. A good-looking screenshot alone does not complete this experiment.

If surfaces double: inspect pose alignment and timing before tuning voxel resolution. If every dimension has the same scale error, inspect depth units and calibration. If shiny or dark regions are missing, compare raw depth there; smoothing cannot recover a measurement the sensor never made.

Then ask what the room looks like

Kerbl and colleagues' Gaussian-splatting work represents a scene with optimized 3D Gaussians and renders them from camera viewpoints. Watch the authors' project video, then identify its objective: reproducing appearance from images. The comparison to your geometric reconstruction is the interesting experiment.

For an implementation route, use Nerfstudio's Splatfacto guide in an isolated environment. Its custom-data workflow needs camera poses and compatible data formatting; recordings do not become a training dataset merely by being saved in a folder. The custom-data guide describes processing images and video, including a COLMAP route. Inspect overlapping, sharp views and camera alignment before fitting a scene.

Your experiment is to reconstruct the same static corner and compare appearance from held-out viewpoints. Look for blurred objects, floaters, and failures away from the capture path. Keep the geometric map as a separate artifact. Installation, conversion, and training of this extension have not been executed for your hardware in this edition; its measured outcome is yours to establish.

Then ask what belongs in the room

ConceptGraphs demonstrates a research route from posed RGB-D images through segmentation, feature extraction, multi-view association, and a 3D object graph. Use its paper and explainer to trace those stages. Its results motivate an experiment; they do not establish accuracy in your house.

Start your own extension with two distinctive objects and a handful of viewpoints. Measure whether observations associate with the correct object, including when one moves or is briefly hidden. Keep “same category” separate from “same physical object.” Then evaluate a few contextual queries against the stored evidence. Add language interfaces only after you can inspect where their answers came from.

Test usefulness before expanding the platform

The commercial hypothesis is that a moving observer can provide useful household information that people would revisit. A first product experiment can test this with the one-room prototype: create a short report showing room layout and evidence-backed sightings of a chosen item. Ask a few prospective users to use the report for a real task, then observe whether they return to it without prompting.

Record time saved or lost, incorrect conclusions, manual corrections, setup effort, and what they actually do next. Compare the workflow with taking a phone photo or measuring the room manually. Interest in a demonstration is different evidence from repeated use. A small team also needs to understand assembly, calibration, support, and maintenance work; the prototype's run log begins to expose those costs.

Make the next investment answer one observed problem: a better sensor for missing geometry, better data for a recurring recognition error, or a clearer interface for a useful query. Pricing and demand remain unvalidated until tested. There is no need to assign a business model to every experiment.

Keep these later projects visible

Transport: a basket carrier needs a new payload, stability, traction, clearance, and stopping assessment. Surveying with a light rover does not qualify its chassis to carry laundry. Start with a measured test load along one controlled route.

Play and exercise: begin with a stationary or slow, turn-based game in a bounded area. Test whether the interaction remains fun after its novelty fades before adding pursuit or faster motion.

Arms and unusual locomotion: the previous edition's joint workshop, wiggle mechanism, and simulation experiments remain archived extensions. Their parts and assumptions belong to those builds. A later learned gait still needs a measured physical baseline, suitable sensing, a simulation model, and a transfer evaluation.

Done means this

You have chosen one extension, written its input requirements and finish check, and kept the working rover revision available. The default is the static-corner reconstruction. Next: save the project so tomorrow starts with an action →

11 · Your project desk

Leave yourself
a way back in.

A useful plan tells you what to do when things work, when they fail, and when you return after a week away.

The exciting part is the robot that understands your home. Today’s work might be measuring a bracket or finding a mislabeled photograph. Your workbench connects that task to the capability it supports and keeps your next action beside the last evidence you saved. Start there when you sit down to build. Use this chapter when you want the full route, the recovery approach, or a backup of your notes.

A focused session gives you a purpose, materials, ordered actions and a finish condition. Its full bench instructions stay available with the required setup and safety information. You can open the chapter for more context or follow the one relevant resource without losing the session you intend to resume.

The first rover has a finish line

Your core project is complete when you can show the fitted assembly, dependable manual motion and stop tests, a checked room map, a short navigation demonstration, an honest model evaluation, and those five real linked observations. The synthetic memory exercise teaches the contract; the real records show that your model and robot data actually meet.

The workbench groups session checks into capabilities and keeps your evidence visible. Chapter checkmarks remain a separate reference record for the ten core chapters, 00–09. A saved experiment can document useful progress even when a check has not passed; only mark a session complete when you can support its finish condition. Chapter 10 is optional research and this project desk is a utility chapter. Neither adds work to the core finish line.

Optional next project · Reconstruct a small part of the room in 3D

Once the core evidence is saved, use Chapter 10's reconstruction experiment to investigate a recorded RGB-D scene. Begin with one corner and compare measured geometry. This is a new experiment with its own entry and exit checks; it does not change whether your first rover project is complete.

The controller bridge, sensor integration and navigation configuration are substantial software projects inside the course. Their interface and acceptance checks are specified; you will still implement and verify them with your hardware. At each integration session, inspect the stated uncertainty and use the smallest listed check to investigate it. Budget several focused sessions for those integrations. A named unknown gives us an experiment to perform; its result tells us whether to continue, adjust a part or revise the plan.

Use the hour you actually have

5 minutes to restart · 40 to build or investigate · 10 to check · 5 to leave a note

Open your workbench and read the saved next action. If you have been away, use Returning after a break to repeat the last small check before extending the system. The focused session keeps its materials, purpose and finish condition together. If you have a short window, use Only ten minutes; that action may prepare the next experiment without completing the whole session.

Before you leave, save what you observed and one exact next action. Include the file, part or measurement you want to open next. Use Save and pause while a check remains unfinished. Choose Record checkpoint met only after saving evidence and confirming that you checked the finish condition. Existing chapter notes and saved-session pins remain available alongside the workbench records.

Keep one artifact: a photograph, a dimension, a trace, a configuration diff, or an error report. Record its local path or describe where to find it; the browser notebook does not collect the file itself. Write why it supports—or fails to support—the claim you were testing. “The program ran” is a different claim from “the robot moved the requested distance.” Both can be useful if we name them accurately.

If you prefer a plain text restart note, this template works too:

Last thing that worked:
Evidence saved at:
What remains uncertain:
Next action, including file / part / chapter:
If that action fails, inspect:
New idea to park for later:

Your notes and progress belong to the browser where you saved them. Use the export controls below to keep a backup or carry them to another device. A break does not erase the evidence you already have; begin by recovering that state.

When a step stops moving

Open the focused session’s I’m stuck help for a diagnostic matched to the current task. If a print or delivery is holding you up, use Waiting for parts to find an available task on the other track. The suggestion depends on the checks you have recorded; inspect its requirements before starting. Keep the unfinished session and its next action saved so you can return when the part arrives.

What is blocking youDefault next action
A print takes hours or parts are in transitUse the prepared parallel-track suggestion. If no next task is ready, save the dependency and use the current session’s small preparation action.
A physical fit failsReturn to the smallest coupon that represents that feature. Measure it, change one parameter, and reprint the coupon.
A driver or bridge does not workSave the exact command and first error, then check its smallest interface with motor output disabled. Work through the first failing acceptance row.
A model performs poorlyInspect five validation errors at the model’s actual image resolution. Name a plausible data or representation problem before changing architecture.
The map bends or jumpsReplay the same bag. Check time, transforms, wheel signs and scan orientation before collecting more data.
The whole project feels too largeOpen the current session and read its finish condition. Use the ten-minute action if that is the window you have, then leave the next action beside your evidence.
A new idea is more excitingCapture it in the workbench’s ideas area: what would it demonstrate, and which capability would it reuse? Its originating session gives you a return point. A local notes/parking-lot.md file also works if you prefer it.

Use agents to accelerate work you can explain

An agent can write a dataset checker or adapt a controller interface quickly. Your learning comes from specifying the observable behavior, predicting a result, and investigating the mismatch. Before accepting a change, explain its inputs, outputs, failure behavior and evidence in your own words. You do not need to type every line to own the experiment.

For a hardware integration, give the agent an interface with measured facts. This is a prompt template, not a motor-control program:

Task: implement one acceptance row from our controller contract.
Inputs: measured wheel geometry, verified count convention,
        exact controller protocol/version, chosen command type.
Behavior: bounded velocity requests; zero on stale commands;
          explicit re-arm after stop; timestamped encoder telemetry.
Deliver: a small diff, mock I/O checks, and an explanation of
         which claims still require a wheels-off-ground bench test.
Do not invent missing pinouts, current ratings, or calibration values.
First explain what evidence would show this row is satisfied.

For the model, ask for a review of split independence, preprocessing, checkpoint selection and the meaning of the metric. Have a second agent inspect the experiment contract before you accept an unexpectedly excellent result. Keep data and code versions with every report so that a later improvement has a fair comparison.

What this edition supplies

The starter downloads include working desktop programs for training an image classifier and querying observation memory, their synthetic checks, practical fit coupons, and measurement worksheets. Their execution evidence is limited to the checks described in the lessons. Synthetic patterns are useful for exercising a pipeline; they do not demonstrate household perception.

The full rover, power system, printed chassis, ROS controller integration, live SLAM and Nav2 behavior require your measured components and physical verification. The book provides a reference architecture and staged acceptance tasks for that work. It does not claim that an unbuilt robot has completed a trip, achieved a measurement accuracy, or recognized your belongings.

A fresh course, with the earlier work preserved. The previous edition contains the original rover, arm, articulated creature and simulated joint experiments. Its browser notes remain separate. This edition starts a new progress record so old checkmarks cannot silently complete different lessons.

Checkpoint: export your notes, identify the last artifact you trust, and leave one exact next action.

Open one resource. Make one thing clearer.

Starting today? Go to the first-hour session and collect your first images. When you open Fusion for the fit coupon, watch sketch constraints. Before training, read the session-split guidance. That is enough reading to begin.

I’d give a reading detour about ten minutes, then try the card’s task. If it raises another question, leave a note and return to the bench. The roadmap below shows the next reference when you need it; it is not a second course to finish first.

Your reading roadmap

The two lanes can advance together. Photos and model training can move forward while a print runs or parts arrive. Arrows show the order within a lane; the tracks meet when you attach your own model’s observations to a checked map.

Build the survey rover

  1. Constrain the couponThen orient it, print it and measure the fit.
  2. Assemble separate componentsUse the actual motor drawing to place the drive.
  3. Measure the supplyThen use the RoboClaw guide for the first powered wheel.
  4. Set up JazzyInspect a stationary scan before mapping.
  5. Draw the framesRecord → build and check a map → navigate in it.

Train the household observer

  1. Separate capture sessionsCollect your distinctive toy present and absent.
  2. Check the training environmentThen train the logistic baseline and read its validation errors.
  3. See how weights learnThen inspect a small convolution.
  4. Trace the CNN training loopCompare it with the baseline on the same split.
  5. Freeze the choice and evaluateKeep the saved model, data split and report together.
Both lanes meet here ↓

Link five real observations to the map. You need a saved model, a mounted camera and checked capture poses. Further 3D reconstruction and language control remain optional branches.

If you want a book beside the bench

For the first physical build, I’d choose Making Things Move. For electrical experiments, use Make: Electronics when a measurement needs more explanation. For training, the free Python edition of An Introduction to Statistical Learning is the main book. Paid books are optional; the free references and supplied exercises support the default route.

Keep the vision in view

We’re working toward a rover you can ask about a room: where it can travel, what it observed, and what evidence supports its answer. A photograph or a fit coupon is a small beginning, but it belongs to that same project. When you want to see the possibilities again, choose one of these companions. You can stop after the idea that interests you; none is a gate to the next session.

Watch · Free · See a small robot become useful

Build a Mobile Robot with ROS: Project Overview

Josh Newans · Articulated Robotics

Watch the opening overview for remote driving, room mapping, and camera-based observations. This gives the separate pieces on your bench a shared destination. The series uses its own robot and software versions; our selected hardware and Jazzy instructions remain your build route.

Bring one idea back: Name the capability you most want to demonstrate, then point to the next session that contributes to it. You do not need to follow the whole series.

Choose your first room and observation →

Listen · Free audio episode · A wider view of mapping

Episode 91 – Robot navigation on land and in water

Robot Talk · Claire Asher interviews John Leonard of MIT

The episode page has an audio player and a downloadable recording. Listen for the relationship between knowing where a robot is and building a map. The discussion of autonomous navigation connects your room survey to questions faced by larger systems.

Bring one idea back: Write one sentence connecting the interview to your rover: for example, why a saved map alone cannot tell it where it is now. Listening is optional; your next build step is still available.

Return to checking your room map →

Read · Free illustrated research article · The longer-term assistant vision

RT-2: New model translates vision and language into action

Google DeepMind

Read the examples connecting camera observations, language, and robot actions. This is a glimpse of a larger research direction, with training data and robot capabilities beyond our first build. Our immediate contribution is to make one observation trustworthy and connect it to a checked capture pose.

Bring one idea back: Write a future request for your rover, then list the observations and tested actions it would need. Keep that request as an idea while you finish the current experiment.

Return to five real observation records →

Make parts that fit

Use the next two resources while your first small part is on the screen or on the bench. The rest answer specific fit, strength, and assembly questions. You do not need to complete an entire CAD course before making your rover.

Video · Free · First CAD session · 9 minutes

Fusion sketch constraints

Autodesk

Watch with your fit coupon open. Focus on the difference between a dimension and a geometric constraint, then fully define the sketch you intend to reuse.

Try it: Change one named clearance. Check that the mounting-hole relationships stay fixed and that the model rebuilds.

Return to the mounting coupon →

Video + illustrated reference · Free · First assembly · 6-minute video

Introduction to Fusion assembly modeling

Autodesk

Watch body-to-component conversion, fixing the base and adding a joint with your deck and mount open. Follow the chapter’s Pin/Ground terminology if your interface differs. For components already in position, use Create an as-built joint and select Rigid for the static mount.

Try it: Make the deck and sensor mount separate components, fix the deck, and constrain their relationship. Change one mount parameter and check that the assembly still makes sense.

Return to your first Fusion assembly →

Illustrated guide · Free · Before the first full-size print

Modeling with 3D printing in mind

Prusa Research

Read orientation, supports, and tolerances. These geometry principles are useful on the X1 Carbon; another printer’s numerical performance is not a tolerance specification for yours.

Try it: Mark the loaded region and the mating surface on a screenshot. Choose an orientation that supports both, or divide the part into a bolted assembly.

Return to the mount and print orientation →

Manufacturer reference · Free · After measuring a fit coupon

X-Y hole and contour compensation

Bambu Lab · Bambu Studio

Use the compensation diagrams when a measured error repeats. Distinguish an enclosed hole from an open slot and an outside contour. Start from the chapter’s saved X1C profile and correct one cause at a time.

Try it: Record the original CAD dimension, measured print, and one proposed change. Reprint the small feature before applying the correction to the chassis.

Return to fit diagnosis →

Video + article · Free · Optional after through-bolts

Tips & Tricks for Heat-Set Inserts used in 3D printing

Stefan Hermann · CNC Kitchen

Watch the installation and alignment. Use the specifications for the exact insert you buy; the internal thread size does not determine its required printed bore.

Try it: Make one sacrificial boss, install an insert, let it cool, and check alignment and resistance to turning before changing your robot design.

Return to the serviceable mount →

Book · Paid · Optional bench reference

Making Things Move: DIY Mechanisms for Inventors, Hobbyists, and Artists

Dustyn Roberts · 1st edition

My first mechanics-book pick for this course. Open Chapter 3’s fastening and joining material while building the chassis. Use Chapter 4’s forces, friction and torque when choosing wheel and motor geometry. Stop when you can explain the load or joint in front of you.

Try it: Trace the weight of the computer through its mount, chassis, wheel supports, and floor. Identify the printed feature carrying each load.

Return to the rolling assembly →

Make motion dependable

The first new electrical skill is measurement: identify the supply, check polarity, and understand what happens when a motor starts or stalls. Read alongside the selected component manuals in the drive chapter.

Book · Paid · Optional practical foundation

Make: Electronics

Charles Platt · 3rd edition

Use the early measurement and component experiments when voltage, current, and resistance are still abstract. Follow an experiment’s specified parts before adapting it to a motor circuit.

Try it: Explain where you would place the meter to measure supply voltage and why current measurement requires a different connection.

Return to the power checks →

Illustrated guide · Free · Before connecting the motor supply

Multimeters

Ladyada · Adafruit Learning System

Read continuity and DC voltage first, with your meter manual beside you. Check the probe sockets and selected mode before touching the circuit.

Try it: With power disconnected, confirm a planned ground connection using continuity. Then follow the chapter’s voltage checks before attaching the motor controller.

Return to the meter and supply checks →

Manufacturer tables + datasheet · Free · During parts selection

The reference motor: Pololu #4885 with encoder

Pololu

Read Dimensions, Using the encoder, and the specifications for this exact 47:1 LP 12V variant. The drawing answers where the motor fits; the electrical and encoder specifications answer how to drive and measure it. Keep the family comparison table for a later redesign.

Try it: Transfer the shaft diameter, mounting pattern, permitted screw engagement, voltage and stall current to the build sheet. Distinguish encoder counts at the motor shaft from counts at the geared output.

Return to the reference parts →

Manufacturer guides · Free · First powered wheel

RoboClaw: connect, measure and save settings

Basicmicro

Use the motor/encoder diagrams and Motion Studio connection instructions beside the chapter’s supported-wheel checks. USB does not power the controller. Read Graphing in Motion Studio when you compare requested and measured speed; use General Settings → Serial → Timeout during interface work.

Try it: Identify the supply, motor and encoder connections, check one encoder’s sign, and save the settings. At the command-timeout session, test fresh-command expiry while status polling continues separately from complete communication loss. The communication timeout alone does not prove both behaviors.

Return to the first encoder and powered wheel →

Train while you build

Start collecting your own images in the first hour. These readings support the small present/absent classifier in Chapter 03. They are not a separate prerequisite course. Your first neural network earns its place by comparison with a simpler trained baseline.

Book · Free author PDF; paid print optional · First model

An Introduction to Statistical Learning: with Applications in Python

Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jonathan Taylor · 2023

For the first visit, read the classification chapter’s logistic-regression explanation beside our baseline. Look back at statistical learning when you need the vocabulary of inputs, targets and error. Save resampling and deep learning for the question that needs them; the chapter’s session-separated split remains our evaluation plan.

Try it: Write the image input, present/absent target, and an example of each type of classification error. Explain why a learned logistic classifier already counts as a trained model.

Return to the trained baseline →

Engineering reference · Free · Before the first fit

Common pitfalls and grouped evaluation

scikit-learn

Read data leakage and preprocessing, then grouped-data evaluation. Nearby frames from one capture run are related. Split complete capture sessions before fitting preprocessing or choosing model settings.

Try it: List the session IDs in training, validation, and test. Confirm they are disjoint, and keep every augmented copy with its source image.

Return to the capture-session split →

Grant Sanderson · 3Blue1Brown

Watch the network explanation, then Gradient descent, how neural networks learn. Translate the handwritten-digit example into our two-class image task. Use the visualization to connect weights, outputs, loss, and updates.

Try it: Point to the trainable parameters in the supplied model and explain what changes during training and what stays fixed during inference.

Return to neural-network training →

Illustrated book section · Free · When the first CNN is ready

Convolutions for Images

Try it: Calculate one output cell from the input and kernel diagram. Find a Conv2d weight in our supplied model and name which values training changes.

Read those examples for the API; run our supplied model in the chapter’s environment. Keep our validation loop and frozen final test separate, even where a tutorial calls recurring evaluation “test.”

Read the mistakes behind the score

This visit is about interpreting the existing report; fitting a calibrator is a later experiment.

Try it: Name one missed toy and one false sighting in your validation results, or record that none occurred in this small set. Average the two class recalls to check balanced accuracy. Explain why score_present=0.9 alone does not establish a 90% chance of being correct.

Join the tracks: remember five real observations

Your next resource is the supplied observation-memory walkthrough and starter. Work through its small synthetic example, then open Session 09B to import five observations from your own model and mounted camera. Keep the image, capture time, model identity, score meaning, map revision and capture pose together.

Finish this step when: a query returns those real records and you can show the evidence for each answer. Here, the capture pose records the rover’s base_link pose when the image was taken; it does not establish the toy’s position. Read depth projection only when you have the measurements needed to calculate an object location. You can complete the core course before adding a scene graph or an LLM.

Later research · Choose one question after the core build

For your first extension, follow reconstruct one corner with recorded RGB-D and known camera poses. After that, choose the question you want to answer: which volume is observed free?, how does the room look from another viewpoint?, which objects relate to each other?, or how can language select a working robot skill? These are separate experiments. Keep one question, one recorded dataset and one acceptance check per detour.

Ask your coding agent for evidence. Have it explain an unfamiliar API, scaffold an experiment, or check a data split. Keep the choice of target, acceptance check, and interpretation in your hands. When a resource introduces five new ideas, capture the four you do not need yet in your workshop notebook.

The selected ROS track is Jazzy. External documentation, video interfaces, package support, and commercial licenses can change; use the chapter’s environment record when reproducing an experiment. No resource recommendation establishes that the physical rover has already been tested.
